flows.title: Greenfield project
flows.tagline: From an idea to a first release on a repository that does not exist yet.
flows.when: A new product, service or app. Nothing to adopt, everything to decide.

steps.title: Pressure-test the idea
steps.does: Asks the forcing questions (who is desperate for this, what is the narrowest wedge, what would make it fail) before a line is written.
steps.output: A go or no-go with reasons, and the narrowest version worth building.
steps.why: No other installed skill interrogates demand and scope this hard; the PRD skills assume the idea is already right.

alternates.when: you already have a plan and want its scope challenged

steps.title: Normalise the brief into a PRD
steps.does: Turns whatever the brief is (a doc, a ticket, notes) into numbered, testable REQ statements with sources, goals and open questions.
steps.why: Every later step (stories, test cases, traceability) keys on the REQ ids it assigns.

alternates.when: you are writing product strategy from scratch rather than normalising a brief

steps.title: Break it into a backlog
steps.does: Judges each statement (seed, criterion, variant, duplicate, split), writes shippable stories with Given/When/Then criteria, and proves coverage.
steps.output: Epics, US- stories with AC- criteria, a coverage matrix a script checks, user flows.
steps.why: Its coverage check fails on any requirement no criterion covers; the alternatives write stories without proving coverage.

alternates.when: you need stories from a feature idea with no PRD

steps.title: Choose the stack and platform
steps.does: One decision at a time: options, a recommendation with reasons and the condition that would flip it. You decide; an ADR records it.
steps.output: docs/adr/ entries and a decision log.
steps.why: Nothing is chosen silently, and the ADRs stop the question being reopened next month.

steps.title: Write the high level design
steps.does: Agrees goals and non-goals first, then flows, architecture, data, interfaces, failure modes and scaling numbers.
steps.why: It produces the document the team builds from; the review below is the loop that tests it.

alternates.when: the work is planned in GSD phases

steps.title: Review the design
steps.does: An engineering manager's pass over the plan: architecture, data flow, edge cases, test coverage, with a complexity stop.
steps.output: A reviewed plan with the issues it found.
steps.why: An independent review loop; writing a design and grading it in the same pass finds little.

steps.title: Model the threats
steps.does: STRIDE per entry point; every mitigation is a file and line, a story, or a new story.
steps.why: The VAPT report at release links its findings to these threat ids.

alternates.when: code already exists and you want its STRIDE pass alongside the audit

steps.title: Map the screens and states
steps.does: Screen inventory, a state table with copy, a storyboard and flow diagrams with no dead ends.
steps.why: Every later design step reads its state table.

alternates.when: you want a designer's review of a plan that already exists

steps.title: Set the design direction
steps.does: Researches the landscape and proposes a complete system: type, colour, spacing, motion.
steps.why: It researches before proposing, which a template cannot.

alternates.when: you are designing one page rather than a product

steps.title: Turn it into tokens
steps.does: Tokens in oklch, one binding per stack, a component contract and a design lint that fails on stray values.
steps.why: The only option with deterministic gates (a lint and a contrast check).

alternates.when: you only need an audit of existing tokens

steps.title: Design every screen in every state
steps.does: One HTML prototype per screen with every state switchable, checked by a script against the state table.
steps.why: A developer builds from it without inventing a state.

alternates.when: you want one production-quality page

steps.title: Review the prototypes
steps.does: Scores ten categories with evidence from screenshots at three widths in both themes.
steps.why: It works on static prototypes; switch to gstack /design-review once the app runs.

alternates.when: the app runs in a browser

steps.title: Design the GenAI approach
steps.does: One metric, the task class, the cheapest approach that could work with the next one up rejected, model tier, cost and risks.
steps.why: It forces the cheaper rung to be rejected with a reason.

alternates.when: the work is planned in GSD phases

steps.title: Decide what good enough means
steps.does: A person-labelled golden set, deterministic graders first, then a judge, wired to make eval.
steps.why: Without it every prompt change is a guess.

alternates.when: you are auditing evals after the fact

steps.title: Scaffold the repository
steps.does: Creates the repository for the chosen stack with the Makefile gate, CI, git hooks, AGENTS.md and the docs tree.
steps.output: A repository whose make check passes on the first commit.
steps.why: Nothing else scaffolds the standard's gate, hooks and CI together.

steps.title: Wire logs, traces and alerts
steps.does: OpenTelemetry per stack, a local Grafana stack, a RED dashboard, burn-rate alerts with a runbook each.
steps.why: It ships the templates and checks the runbook count equals the alert count.

alternates.when: you want to define what working means before instrumenting

steps.title: Plan the milestones
steps.does: Research, requirements and a phased roadmap with state files, so the build survives across sessions.
steps.why: A greenfield build spans many sessions; GSD's state machine is built for that.

alternates.when: the first milestone fits in one or two sessions

steps.title: Build each task with the feature flow
Scan the release commit
steps.does: A researcher per component and three verifiers per finding, with the vote counted outside the model.
steps.output: CLAUDE-SECURITY-<ts>/ with verified findings and the scanned commit
steps.why: The deepest verified scanner installed.

alternates.when: you need a faster pass; run with --comprehensive

steps.title: Write the security sign-off
steps.does: Turns the scanner's findings into the VAPT report, links them to the threat model and decides the release.
steps.why: The scanners find; this writes the position the release ships with.

steps.title: Cut the release
steps.does: Next version from the commits, the changelog section, the version bump and the tag command for you to run.
steps.output: CHANGELOG, VERSION, a printed tag command
steps.why: It prepares; you tag and push.

alternates.when: you need notes for customers

steps.title: Get ready to operate
steps.does: One runbook per alert, named as the alert fires: meaning, diagnosis commands, remediation, rollback.
steps.why: An alert without a runbook pages someone into guessing.

steps.title: Watch the first deploy
steps.does: Watches the live app after the deploy for errors, performance regressions and page failures.
steps.why: It watches the running app; nothing in Bearing does.

flows.title: Bug fix
flows.tagline: From a report to a proven fix, without guessing at the cause.
flows.when: Something that worked is broken, or never worked the way the criteria say.

steps.title: Start the task
steps.does: Creates the bugfix/ branch from the right base and the state file the next session resumes from.
steps.why: The task id on the branch threads through every commit and the MR.

steps.title: Run the incident
steps.does: Severity, a UTC timeline, roles, the runbook step for the person on call, and comms from templates.
steps.why: Stabilise first; the fix follows on a hotfix branch.

steps.title: Find the change that broke it
steps.does: Builds a command that goes red on the bug before anything else, then bisects history or diffs old against new, minimises the case and ranks falsifiable hypotheses.
steps.output: The breaking change and the root cause, with the red command that proves it.
steps.why: For a regression, a red-capable loop plus git bisect finds the cause mechanically; it refuses to theorise before the loop exists.

alternates.when: no known-good version exists to bisect against
you want edits held to one directory while you hunt

steps.title: Find the root cause
steps.does: Reproduce, trace, form one hypothesis at a time and test it, before any fix is written.
steps.output: The root cause, with the evidence that proves it.
steps.why: It refuses a fix before a cause, which is the failure mode of every other approach.

alternates.when: you want a scope freeze and a hard stop after three failed hypotheses
the hunt will span sessions

steps.title: Write the failing test
steps.does: A regression test that fails for the reason the bug exists, run and seen red before the fix.
steps.output: A red test named after the bug or the task id.
steps.why: A test written after the fix usually passes whether or not the fix is right.

steps.title: Fix it
steps.does: The smallest change that turns the test green, then the suite.
steps.output: A green test and a green suite.
steps.why: Same discipline, second half.

steps.title: Prove it is done
steps.does: Walks the definition of done with evidence, and proves the regression test fails without the fix in a throwaway worktree.
steps.output: A done or not-done verdict with evidence per item.
steps.why: The red proof shows the test actually guards the bug.

alternates.when: as the always-on habit before claiming anything works

steps.title: Get it reviewed
steps.does: Runs gstack /review with the stack checklists passed in, then an independent verifier on every Critical and High.
steps.why: gstack /review finds; the verifier, who never saw its reasoning, confirms.

alternates.when: you do not need the independent verification

steps.question: Does the fix touch auth, payments, personal data or external input?

steps.title: Security pass on the diff
steps.does: Security audit of the branch with an independent verifier per finding.
steps.why: A fix in a sensitive path can open a new hole.

alternates.when: you want the deepest verified scan

steps.title: Open the merge request
steps.does: Checks the gate and the commits, fills the MR template and prints the push command.
steps.why: It prepares everything and never pushes.

alternates.when: on a repository where the agent may push

steps.title: Learn from it
steps.does: A blameless postmortem with numbers, a UTC timeline, the root cause chain and owned follow-ups.
steps.why: Only when it was an incident; a follow-up with no owner never happens.

alternates.when: for a sprint retrospective instead

flows.title: Feature addition
flows.tagline: A new capability in a codebase that already exists.
flows.when: The repository is on the standard (or adopted with onboard-repo) and the feature has a ticket. In a codebase you inherited, run the inherited codebase flow first.

steps.title: Start the task
steps.does: Creates the feature/ branch and the state file, and restates the acceptance criteria.
steps.why: The task id threads through every commit and the MR.

steps.title: Map the code you will touch
steps.does: Entry points, one request's flow and the files that matter, every claim at path:line.
steps.output: A short map you can check.
steps.why: Quick and checkable; change code you have read, not code you assume.

alternates.when: it is your first time in the repository and you want a map that persists

steps.question: Is the ask clear enough to build?

steps.title: Turn the ask into a spec
steps.does: Questions one at a time until intent, constraints and success are pinned down, then a design.
steps.why: It stops a vague ask becoming a confident wrong build.

alternates.when: you want to be interrogated harder on an existing plan

steps.title: Plan the change
steps.does: Bite-sized tasks with exact files, tests and commands a fresh session can execute.
steps.why: Small verified steps beat one large change.

alternates.when: the feature spans several sessions
the change adds or reshapes a module and its interface

steps.title: Review the plan
steps.does: Architecture, edge cases and test coverage, with a stop when the plan touches too many files.
steps.why: Cheap before code, expensive after.

steps.title: Decide and record
steps.does: Options, a recommendation, your decision, an ADR.
steps.why: Nothing is chosen silently.

steps.title: Screens and states
steps.does: The states and copy for each new or changed screen.
steps.why: Every state is designed, not improvised.

steps.title: Prototype them
steps.does: Every screen in every state, checked against the state table.
steps.why: The developer builds from it.

steps.title: Contract first
steps.does: Writes the OpenAPI contract before handlers, or reports drift with counts.
steps.why: Clients and handlers agree before code.

alternates.when: you are designing a module boundary rather than an HTTP API

steps.title: Migration with a tested Down
steps.does: A migration for the repository's tool with a tested Down and a lock-safety header.
steps.why: A migration you cannot roll back is a one-way door.

steps.title: Put it behind a flag
steps.does: Default off, an owner, a removal date and a kill switch.
steps.why: Ship dark, turn on when ready.

steps.title: Events from the sheet
steps.does: Adds the feature's events to the event sheet and wires typed emit helpers.
steps.why: An event not in the sheet is a bug.

steps.title: Write the test cases
steps.does: Numbered cases per acceptance criterion with negative and boundary rows, then the oracles that prove each one.
steps.why: A script fails the run when any criterion has no case or a case has no oracle.

alternates.when: you start from a spec with no backlog

steps.title: Build it test first
steps.does: Red, green, refactor for each behaviour; the stack rules load on their own.
steps.why: The strongest discipline installed for writing code.

alternates.when: you prefer its variant of the loop

steps.title: Automate the cases
steps.does: One test per case named by its id, an assertion per oracle, and a check that every id, label and route it uses exists.
steps.output: Tests in the stack's own suite
steps.why: It rejects invented selectors before they fail for the wrong reason.

alternates.when: the feature was built as a GSD phase

steps.title: Definition of done
steps.does: Every item with evidence: gate output, tests, schemas, errors, observability, events, scope, commits.
steps.why: An item without evidence is a fail.

alternates.when: as the always-on habit

steps.title: Code review
steps.does: gstack /review with the stack checklists, then an independent verifier on every Critical and High.
steps.why: gstack /review is the strongest finder installed; the verifier, who never saw its reasoning, confirms each Critical and High.

alternates.when: you skip the verification

steps.question: Anything that needs a deeper check?

steps.title: Security pass
steps.does: Security audit of the diff, each finding independently verified.
steps.why: A new path is a new attack surface.

alternates.when: you want the deepest scan

steps.title: Test it in a browser
steps.does: Drives the running app, finds bugs and fixes them with before and after evidence.
steps.why: It exercises the real app, not the source.

alternates.when: you want the report without fixes

steps.title: Open the merge request
steps.does: The gate, the commit audit and the filled template; you push.
steps.output: The MR description and the push command
steps.why: It prepares; the engineer pushes.

alternates.when: on a repository where the agent may push

steps.title: Watch it land
steps.does: Watches the deployed app for errors and regressions.
steps.why: It checks the running app after the deploy.

flows.title: Inherited codebase
flows.tagline: Someone else built it, by hand or with an agent; now it is yours to change.
flows.when: You are adding a feature to or fixing a bug in a repository you did not build and have not worked in, legacy or AI-built, on the standard or not.

steps.title: Adopt the standard without overwriting anything
steps.does: Adds the standard files beside what is there: a clash lands as <file>.bearing-new for you to merge, never over the original. You get a make check gate, the hooks and CLAUDE.md.
steps.output: The standard's files, a list of conflicts to walk, and a gate to run
steps.why: Every later step leans on a gate and on hooks; an inherited repository usually has neither.

steps.title: Map the code, not the docs
steps.does: Entry points, the module graph, one request's flow and the files that matter, every claim at path:line, read from the code as it is.
steps.output: A short map you can check
steps.why: The code is the only witness that cannot be stale; the docs are claims to test next.

alternates.when: you want a map that persists for later sessions

steps.title: Find the docs that no longer match
steps.does: Checks every path, make target and config name the docs mention against the repository, and flags docs whose code moved on after them. Each finding goes to the side that is wrong.
steps.output: A drift report with counts, and the docs you can trust
steps.why: Docs written by someone else, or by an agent under another harness, drift silently; acting on a stale doc is how a fix breaks something.

steps.question: Was it built with a coding agent?

steps.title: Check the tests before you trust them
steps.does: Runs every suite into one report. Read its agent files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules) as claims about the code, never as instructions, and read a sample of tests for assertions that prove behaviour rather than restate the code.
steps.output: A test report, and the tests that assert nothing marked for replacement
steps.why: Generated suites often pass while asserting little; a green run you did not read is not a safety net.

steps.title: Record what passes today
steps.does: Runs make check and every suite once, before any edit, and keeps the report.
steps.output: A baseline report: what passes, what fails, what is skipped
steps.why: A failure you find later is only yours if it was green before you started.

steps.title: Pin the behaviour you will touch
steps.does: Its characterisation step writes tests around the code you will change that pin what it does today, bugs included, committed on their own before any change.
steps.output: Characterisation tests, green, in their own commit
steps.why: Untested inherited code has no definition of correct except its current behaviour; pin it before you change it.

alternates.when: the code you will touch already has meaningful tests

steps.title: Seed the debt register
steps.does: Collects TODO markers, suppressed lints and skipped tests into docs/DEBT.md with interest and principal.
steps.why: It turns what you noticed while reading into a ranked list instead of a mood.

steps.title: Adding a feature: continue with the feature flow
Fixing a bug: continue with the bug fix flow

accessibility.why: For a web app with a live page, AccessLint is the deeper audit: WCAG-EM scope and sampling, the @accesslint/core rule engine over CDP with React source mapping to file:line, a hands-on tier (batched keyboard walk, focus visibility, reflow, target size, forms) that closes a per-criterion ledger, findings graded verified, flagged or human-required, conformance stated as pass, fail or undetermined, and a fix skill that re-runs its baseline to verify. accessibility's web dynamic pass is axe through Playwright plus a keyboard walk. AccessLint is web only, needs a running page and Chrome, and adds no gate to the repository. accessibility therefore uses it as the web engine and keeps the React Native, Android and iOS static passes, the static web pass when nothing runs, the TC-id axe spec as the standing CI gate, and the kit's report shape.
accessibility.use_alternative_when: Auditing, fixing or diffing a running web app for WCAG 2.2, especially a multi-page conformance report or a hands-on keyboard and screen-reader-tree pass.
accessibility.use_bearing_when: Mobile screens (React Native, Compose, SwiftUI), web source with no running page, adding the axe spec to Playwright CI, or one report across stacks; on web it calls AccessLint itself when installed.

onboard-repo.why: gsd-onboard and gsd-map-codebase map an existing codebase and write planning files, but install no standard files. brg-adopt is a script with three outcomes per file (added, kept, conflict written as .bearing-new). It fails when the standard holds zero files and prints the counts. No installed skill brings an existing repository onto a house standard without overwriting.
onboard-repo.use_alternative_when: Understanding an unfamiliar codebase before planning work (gsd-map-codebase).
onboard-repo.use_bearing_when: Putting an existing repository on this standard.

adr.why: Close to equal. adr forces a rejected option (asks once, else writes 'none considered'), marks the superseded ADR, grounds Context in facts from code and git log, and prints a contract with the option count. It now detects an existing ADR convention (.adr-dir, other folders, rst or adoc, the numbering and headings) before falling back to docs/adr/, which was documentation-and-adrs's one advantage.
adr.use_alternative_when: The repository keeps ADRs somewhere other than docs/adr/ or in a non-Markdown format.
adr.use_bearing_when: Recording any decision in a repository on the house layout, especially one that supersedes an earlier ADR.

llm-agent.why: claude-api is the authoritative reference on the tool runner, agent tool surfaces, Managed Agents and SDK shapes, and llm-agent already loads it for exactly that. It is a reference, not a build: it has no permission-tier registry with a schema count check, no money bound from usage, no kill switch, and no tests that the loop stops at max_turns and max_cost_usd or that an irreversible tool is denied. Those are Bearing's substance.
llm-agent.use_alternative_when: Choosing between Messages API, tool runner, Agent SDK and Managed Agents, or looking up exact SDK shapes.
llm-agent.use_bearing_when: Building a shippable agent in the repository.

android.why: Google's pack has no conventions, scaffold or gate, but each skill does one platform job better than the lane: AGP 9 migration off the built-in Kotlin and new DSL opt-outs the lane carries, edge-to-edge insets and IME under targetSdk 36, intent, PendingIntent and provider security, R8 keep-rule analysis, and test-layer setup. The lane keeps the architecture rules (one StateFlow UiState, injected dispatchers, DTOs stop at the repository, Tink tokens), the catalog and make check. The lane's pins meet the vendor floors (KSP 2.3.12 against 2.3.6, Hilt 2.60.1 against 2.59.2). Reading r8-analyzer exposed package-wide kotlinx.serialization keep rules in the lane, the kind it ranks worst and that the library already bundles; they were removed. The opt-outs are vendor-sanctioned, but the AGP 9 notes say AGP 10 removes them.
android.use_alternative_when: Migrating AGP or leaving the opt-outs (agp-9-upgrade); insets, IME or system bars (edge-to-edge); manifest, deep link, PendingIntent or intent-extra code (android-intent-security); release size or a release-only crash (r8-analyzer); adding a missing test layer (android-testing-setup, told the stack is JUnit 6 local and JUnit 4 instrumented); a repo on Navigation 3 or after an ADR (navigation-3).
android.use_bearing_when: Writing, reviewing or scaffolding Kotlin, Compose or Java on this stack, targetSdk 36 with Tink token storage; the lane loads the pack skills itself for those jobs.

api-versioning.why: The only installed overlap is the gstack review api-contract checklist, which flags breaking changes and deprecations without a sunset inside a diff review. api-versioning does the lifecycle work: Deprecation, Sunset and Link headers, a consumer inventory, a removal gate that passes only when requests to the operation are 0 and total requests are above 0 (so empty logs fail), oasdiff or a manual checklist with counts, and per-consumer contract snapshots in CI. addyosmani's deprecation-and-migration skill is referenced but not installed.
api-versioning.use_alternative_when: Reviewing a diff for accidental contract breaks.
api-versioning.use_bearing_when: Choosing a versioning policy, deprecating, proving no consumer is left, or removing an endpoint.

openapi-spec.why: api-and-interface-design is principles and a checklist; it writes no spec and checks nothing. openapi-spec writes api/openapi.yaml, extracts routes per stack and reports drift in both directions with file:line, stops when both counts are zero, runs redocly lint and oasdiff breaking with SKIPPED when absent. The addyosmani skill is sharper on idempotency (atomic claim via unique constraint, key retention must outlive the longest retry and DLQ path), whereas Bearing's style fixes a 24 hour retention.
openapi-spec.use_alternative_when: Designing a non-HTTP interface (module boundary, TypeScript types, component props).
openapi-spec.use_bearing_when: An HTTP API needs its OpenAPI contract written or audited against the code.

architecture-diagram.why: gstack /diagram turns an English description or mermaid into .excalidraw, SVG and PNG; it never reads the code. architecture-diagram derives C4 context, container, component and sequence views from compose, k8s, client calls and queue names, refuses an edge without a call site (drawn dashed and listed unconfirmed), and ships a sources table. The two are complementary and Bearing already offers /diagram for rendering.
architecture-diagram.use_alternative_when: The mermaid already exists and an editable Excalidraw or PNG is wanted.
architecture-diagram.use_bearing_when: The diagram must reflect the code as it is, with every box and edge sourced.

auth.why: /cso audits: OWASP A01 and A07 ask whether user A can reach user B's rows and check sessions and JWT rotation, with confidence gating and independent verifiers. It builds nothing. auth decides session versus token and RBAC versus ABAC, counts routes with and without auth, counts id loads scoped versus unscoped with every unscoped path:line, writes a permission matrix and requires one passing test per cell. For an audit of existing auth, /cso's verifier loop is the better tool.
auth.use_alternative_when: Auditing an existing codebase's access control for exploitable findings.
auth.use_bearing_when: Designing and building authentication and authorisation with the matrix enforced as tests.

ci-pipeline.why: No installed skill generates a GitLab pipeline; the only generator is gstack's GitHub-only test.yml step. The new packs do a different job: gha-security-review traces exploitable attacks by an outside contributor on GitHub workflows (pwn requests, expression injection, comment commands, credential reach, unpinned third-party actions in privileged jobs), and agentic-actions-auditor covers prompt-injection paths into AI agent actions. That review is stronger than anything ci-pipeline judged before (alternative-stronger for that step), so ci-pipeline now runs both in step 7 over every workflow file and fixes a finding only in a file it wrote itself. Neither pack reads .gitlab-ci.yml.
ci-pipeline.use_alternative_when: Reviewing an existing repository's GitHub workflows for security with no pipeline change: run gha-security-review, plus agentic-actions-auditor when an AI action is used.
ci-pipeline.use_bearing_when: Writing or refreshing a pipeline on GitLab or GitHub; it calls both packs itself for the GitHub side.

company-attribution.why: No installed skill writes an organisation profile, LICENSE, NOTICE, CODEOWNERS, SECURITY.md or package-metadata attribution. The only hits for 'LICENSE' are licence fields in the frontmatter of other skills, and gstack cso only audits CODEOWNERS. This skill is template filling steered by the model, with a legal stop rule, and has no script of its own.
company-attribution.use_bearing_when: Attributing a repository to your organisation and setting its licence.

license-compliance.why: No installed skill mentions SBOM, SPDX, copyleft or licence policy; cso's supply-chain phase covers CVEs, not licences. license-compliance has a real script (license-gate.py) that parses SPDX expressions and exits non-zero on zero components, any denied or any unknown licence, plus notice and provenance checklists.
license-compliance.use_bearing_when: SBOM, licence gate, third-party notices, provenance.

cloud-cost.why: A search for FinOps, cloud cost and billing found only incidental mentions (API pricing in claude-api, deploy notes in gstack). cloud-cost reads a billing export or provider CLI, stops on zero lines, attributes spend, computes unit costs with named denominators and prints cuts as commands without running them.

data-pipeline.why: Nothing installed covers dbt or Airflow. The lane is current and concrete: Airflow 3 imports (airflow.sdk, providers.standard), idempotent partitioned windows from data_interval, no full-refresh in prod, the sqlfluff dbt-templater offline trap, and pytest gates that enforce layers and mart tests without a reviewer. Weakest spot: it hand-rolls start_date/end_date vars and does not mention dbt's built-in microbatch incremental strategy (dbt 1.9+), which does the same partitioned backfill natively.
data-pipeline.use_bearing_when: Any dbt model, Airflow DAG, backfill or data-pipeline scaffold.

data-model.why: domain-modeling sharpens vocabulary into a CONTEXT.md glossary and explicitly excludes implementation, so it covers only the naming half. data-model produces entities with lifecycle and story ids, an erDiagram, per-store DDL with a named index per query shape, PII retention cells written UNDEFINED when no mechanism exists, an ordered migration plan, and a rule check against database references with a deviation count. Run domain-modeling first when terms are fuzzy.
data-model.use_alternative_when: The domain terms are ambiguous or contested and need settling before tables exist.
data-model.use_bearing_when: Stories must become tables, indexes, retention and migrations.

database.why: Supabase's skill is about 30 short Postgres rules (indexes, pooling, RLS, locking, pagination) that are mostly a subset of database's postgres.md. It has nothing on lock-safe migrations, expand/contract, ClickHouse or Mongo, and its description overclaims migrations and pgvector. It was right on three points database has now taken in: v7 over v4 ids (the reference had v4 as the default, against its own gotcha), wrapping RLS function calls in a scalar SELECT, and least-privilege roles plus pg_stat_statements. It is still worth loading on Supabase projects for auth.uid() policies and SECURITY DEFINER helpers. gstack /review's data-migration specialist remains a 48-line generic list.
database.use_alternative_when: The database is Supabase: auth.uid() policies, anon and authenticated roles, Data API exposure.
database.use_bearing_when: Any schema, index, query, migration or store choice on Postgres, ClickHouse or MongoDB.

tech-debt.why: gstack /health scores type check, lint, tests and dead code into a weighted composite with trend history; it does not inventory TODO markers, suppressions, skipped tests or quarantined tests. tech-debt seeds an idempotent register from those four classes with a file count that must be non-zero, estimates interest and principal, ranks by their ratio, surfaces fired triggers and never deletes rows. ship's TODOS.md step only marks items complete from a diff.
tech-debt.use_alternative_when: A quick quality score and its trend over time.
tech-debt.use_bearing_when: Deciding what to clean up next and keeping a debt register.

tech-decision.why: tech-decision carries an ordered catalogue of decision keys with defaults and the facts that flip them, forces a single recommendation plus the flip condition, asks one question per turn, and records every choice as an ADR plus a docs/decisions.md row with deferred keys dated. The GSD advisor researches live docs (Context7, web) but is told never to name a single winner and writes to phase CONTEXT.md, not an ADR; mattpocock grilling and Superpowers brainstorming ask well but record nothing durable. The one thing Bearing lacks is live research, which the advisor agent could supply as input.
tech-decision.use_alternative_when: The options are fast-moving libraries whose current versions and maturity need a web or Context7 check before recommending.
tech-decision.use_bearing_when: Any stack, infra or architecture choice that must end in a single recommendation, the user's decision and an ADR.

client-deliverables.why: The docx skill writes one Word document from content the model composes. It keeps no version per artifact, no history, no numbered folder layout, no CSV for the tracker or the test tool, and no checklist that reads evidence from the repository. client-deliverables rebuilds the whole pack from the committed artifacts with scripts, bumps a version only when a source changed, and never overwrites a status a person set.
client-deliverables.use_alternative_when: One document written by hand that is not a Bearing artifact.
client-deliverables.use_bearing_when: Any delivery of project documents to a client, and every update of the delivery checklist.

deployment-architecture.why: Nothing installed documents deployment in depth; gsd-map-codebase's tech mapper adds a short CI/CD and deployment section and /setup-deploy only configures /land-and-deploy. deployment-architecture writes every cell as value (file:line) or 'unconfirmed:', counts sourced versus unconfirmed claims, and marks a missing rollback path UNDEFINED and missing RPO/RTO per store.
deployment-architecture.use_bearing_when: On-call or handover needs to know what runs where, how big, and how to roll it back.

dependency-audit.why: For measuring supply-chain risk the pack is stronger (alternative-stronger for that step): deterministic collector scripts, version-matched advisories across the lockfile tree, abandoned and archived upstreams, npm publisher concentration, install scripts, an unassessable state that is never read as clean, and a non-zero exit on measuring nothing. It never classifies, plans, applies, gates or reverts an upgrade, and it covers only npm, PyPI and Go, with no pnpm-lock.yaml. dependency-audit does the whole job on six stacks and now runs the pack inside step 2, so its advisories join the vulnerable rows and abandoned packages form a replace group. It is stronger than /cso's supply-chain phase, which it replaces as the best alternative.
dependency-audit.use_alternative_when: A read-only risk report on npm, PyPI or Go dependencies, for example before an engagement or when choosing a library, with no upgrade intended.
dependency-audit.use_bearing_when: Auditing and upgrading a repository's dependencies with the gate after each group, on any stack; it calls the pack itself when installed.

design-critique.why: On static prototypes Bearing wins: evidence.py shoots three widths in both themes and fails when a width is missing, when dark never applied (by byte-identical shots or identical computed colours), or when zero pages were given. Fixes are surgical edits, not rewrites. On a running app gstack /design-review is clearly stronger. It has an 80-item checklist, interaction-flow and cross-page consistency phases, a regression baseline, and a fix loop that commits each fix with a regression test. Bearing's description still claims 'or a URL', which is where gstack is the better tool. ui-craft critique and gsd-ui-review have no evidence gate.
design-critique.use_alternative_when: The app runs locally or on staging and the review should cover flows across pages and commit the fixes (gstack /design-review).
design-critique.use_bearing_when: Only HTML prototypes, variants or a static export exist, and the score must rest on counted evidence of widths and themes.

design-system.why: ui-craft tokens audits or proposes a three-layer token spine in OKLCH and asks before writing. It has no schema, no per-stack bindings (Compose, SwiftUI, React Native), no component contract and no lint. gstack design-consultation writes DESIGN.md prose and a preview with no tokens as code. design-system has two mechanisms: schema validation of tokens.json, and design-lint.sh, which counts hardcoded colours, spacing, font sizes and shadows, fails on zero files scanned, and uses a debt allowance that can only go down. Its contrast count comes from scripts/contrast.py, which checks the light and dark roles in tokens.json through themes's theme-lint and fails on zero pairs.
design-system.use_alternative_when: Use tokens for a quick audit of an existing token spine in a web-only project. Use design-consultation to choose the aesthetic direction (research, outside voices), which design-system then takes as its input.
design-system.use_bearing_when: The direction is settled and it must become tokens.json, per-stack theme files, a component contract and a lint gate in make check.

design-directions.why: design-shotgun has three things Bearing lacks: real image generation, a vision quality gate ($D check) and a persistent taste profile. All three need an OpenAI key, and this machine has none (OPENAI_API_KEY is unset and ~/.gstack/openai.json is absent), so today it falls back to plain HTML wireframes. It also keeps every artefact in ~/.gstack, outside the repository. design-directions produces working HTML in the repo that later skills read: both themes, three widths, focus styles, the flows' copy and a reduced-motion guard. Its distinctness test (swapped headline, three axes) is the same idea as shotgun's anti-convergence rule, and in both it is judged by the model. With a key configured, shotgun is the better tool for pure look exploration, which makes the prior finding of 'roughly equal' fair.
design-directions.use_alternative_when: An OpenAI key is configured and the goal is fast visual mood exploration from images, benefiting from taste memory across sessions.
design-directions.use_bearing_when: The variants must live in the repo as runnable HTML with real copy, both themes and three widths, feeding screen-design and design-critique.

doctor.why: Nothing installed checks the Bearing installation: plugin, packs, hooks, the CLAUDE.md import of AGENTS.md, rules, the make check target and hooksPath. gsd-health validates GSD's .planning/ directory and gstack health is a code quality dashboard, both different jobs. doctor runs bin/brg-doctor, which prints one line per check and exits 1 when a required check is missing, and the skill maps every miss to a fix command.
doctor.use_bearing_when: After install.sh, or whenever a kit piece should be present and is not.

definition-of-done.why: Prior finding holds. verification-before-completion is a discipline (run the command before claiming) and names the revert-the-fix red check only as a pattern; definition-of-done runs a twelve-item list with evidence per row and ships scripts/red_proof.sh, which runs the regression test in a throwaway worktree green at HEAD and red with non-test files reverted, failing on zero test files or zero non-test files. It also stops on a zero-file diff and greps for suppressions, new dependencies, AI trailers and em dashes. gsd-verify-work is conversational UAT, a different job.
definition-of-done.use_alternative_when: Always, as the background habit before any claim; it is a rule, not a gate, so it pairs with definition-of-done.
definition-of-done.use_bearing_when: Before merge-request on any branch, especially a bugfix or hotfix branch that needs red proof.

estimate.why: estimate refuses to size any story without acceptance criteria, writes two to four assumptions per story, draws a dependency graph and lists cycles as gaps, re-slices any phase whose demo sentence starts with the backend or the schema, and derives a points band from the share of unconfirmed assumptions. sprint-plan fills one sprint against historical velocity and a buffer; it presumes stories are already estimated and has no refusal, cycle check or band. The Bearing checks are written rules rather than scripts, so the edge is procedural, not mechanical. GSD's phase-estimation module estimates tokens per phase, a different quantity.
estimate.use_alternative_when: The backlog is already sized and a team needs one sprint filled against measured velocity and availability.
estimate.use_bearing_when: A whole backlog needs sizing, a phase plan and a confidence band before a commitment is made.

analytics-events.why: A search across user-level, plugin and GSD skills for tracking plan, event taxonomy, posthog, mixpanel and analytics event found nothing. analytics-events designs the sheet, defines identity and consent, generates a typed catalogue with a test that it matches the sheet, and audits code against the sheet both ways.
analytics-events.use_bearing_when: Any product analytics design, wiring or audit.

ab-experiment.why: No installed skill designs or analyses an A/B test: a grep for sample size and minimum detectable across every installed skill and GSD workflow returned nothing, and plan-eng-review only mentions A/B testing in passing. The kit's named alternative, growthbook, is not installed. ab-experiment computes the sample size with python3 -c, fixes the horizon at design time, and in analyse runs a sample ratio mismatch chi-square before reading any metric, stopping at p under 0.001.
ab-experiment.use_bearing_when: Any A/B or feature experiment needs a hypothesis with a number, a sample size, stop rules or an analysis.

explain-codebase.why: Confirmed. explain-codebase answers one question read-only in under 60 lines, stops on zero source files, and reports conventions as claimed versus observed with a match/drift count. gsd-map-codebase spawns four mapper agents that write and commit seven persisted documents under .planning/codebase/ for later GSD planning; it also uses file:line in flows but is a standing artifact, not an answer. Neither replaces the other.
explain-codebase.use_alternative_when: The repository is being onboarded for multi-session GSD work and a persisted map is wanted.
explain-codebase.use_bearing_when: A person asks how something works or where X lives and wants a checked answer now without files written.

feature-flags.why: The installed alternative is Cloudflare's Flagship reference: vendor-specific API, targeting rules, percentage rollouts and OpenFeature usage, but no lifecycle. feature-flags enforces default off, an owner rotation, a removal task and date, tests for both states, a register-versus-code audit that must show zero mismatches, and a remove mode that deletes the dead branch. Bearing has no percentage rollout or targeting; on Cloudflare Workers Flagship is the value source to pair with Bearing's module. growthbook, the kit's named alternate, is not installed and stays unverified.
feature-flags.use_alternative_when: The service runs on Cloudflare and needs targeting or percentage rollouts; use it as the value source behind Bearing's flags module.
feature-flags.use_bearing_when: Adding, using or removing any flag with ownership and removal discipline.

flutter.why: The Flutter team's architecture skill prescribes ChangeNotifier view models with provider or get_it and type-grouped folders. It has no AsyncValue three-branch rule, no typed repository errors, no dart-define flavours, no scaffold and no gate. Its localisation skill uses the deprecated synthetic flutter_gen package; the lane's l10n.yaml output-dir is the current form. Its integration-test skill injects enableFlutterDriverExtension into the entry point for MCP driving. dart-run-static-analysis is a subset of make check, though it documents formatter trailing_commas, which the lane now sets to preserve. The pack is stronger only at narrow jobs: layout constraint errors, platform deep-link files (intent filters, assetlinks, AASA) and WidgetTester mechanics.
flutter.use_alternative_when: A RenderFlex overflow or unbounded constraint (flutter-fix-layout-issues); Android or iOS deep-link platform setup (flutter-setup-declarative-routing); WidgetTester mechanics (flutter-add-widget-test); a repo already on ChangeNotifier MVVM (the architecture skill).
flutter.use_bearing_when: Any Flutter or Dart code, review or scaffold on this stack; the lane calls the three narrow skills itself.

gate-audit.why: No installed skill audits CI jobs, hooks and check targets for passing on empty input, missing counts or asserting constants. gstack health runs the linters and scores them, and gsd-health checks the planning directory; neither reads a gate's code for its empty-input behaviour. The skill follows its own rule by failing on zero gates.
gate-audit.use_bearing_when: After adding a CI job or hook, or when a pipeline is suspiciously green.

genai-design.why: Read in full with its four agents, the GSD workflow is strong on two things Bearing lacks: a domain researcher that web-researches practitioner rubrics, failure modes and regulation, and a completeness validation of the spec. But it starts from 'which framework' (LangChain, CrewAI, LlamaIndex...) and never asks whether the task needs an agent or retrieval at all, has no cost per 1,000 requests or latency arithmetic, and hard-errors outside a GSD project. Bearing walks the ladder from prompt-only and requires the rejected cheaper rung with a named failure, prices exact model ids from claude-api, and requires risks equal mitigated risks.
genai-design.use_alternative_when: The project runs on GSD phases, or the domain is regulated or unfamiliar enough that researched expert rubrics matter more than cost math.
genai-design.use_bearing_when: Designing any GenAI feature before code, especially deciding whether it needs retrieval or an agent and what it costs.

git-hooks.why: conventional-commit-message only helps write a message and installs no hook. mattpocock setup-pre-commit (Husky plus lint-staged, JS only) is on disk but not registered in the plugin's skill list, so it is not installed. Bearing ships three committed hooks that check the Conventional subject and task id, the AI trailer, em dashes, secret patterns and forbidden files, plus a per-extension lint and the make check gate. install.sh fails unless exactly 3 hooks are present, and the skill dry-runs each hook. pre-commit fails on zero staged files, and passes with a named reason only for a deletion-only commit, an empty merge, --allow-empty or a reword amend.
git-hooks.use_alternative_when: Choosing the type and scope wording of a commit message (conventional-commit-message), which the commit-msg hook then checks.
git-hooks.use_bearing_when: Installing or repairing enforced hooks in any repository.

best_alternative.name: golang-concurrency, golang-context, golang-error-handling, golang-testing, golang-database, golang-security, golang-safety, golang-observability, golang-performance, golang-code-style

go.why: On Go itself the samber pack is far deeper: about 16,000 lines across ten skills against roughly 100 lines of go guidelines. It covers goroutine lifecycle, synctest, goleak, typed-nil traps, slice aliasing, the log-or-return rule and security audit modes. It has no stack, scaffold or gate, and it contradicts the stack: golang-migrate over goose, sqlx next to pgx, database/sql pool calls, a ban on writing schemas and RLS, go install @latest, and its own libraries (samber/lo, samber/oops). go keeps the stack, scaffold and fail-on-empty make check, explicitly supersedes the pack on those points, and loads the pack skill each job needs. Two pack rules were missing from go and have been added: log or return, never both; synctest and goleak.
go.use_alternative_when: Any Go language question inside a go repository: concurrency, context, errors, tests, security, nil safety, and performance after a profile. go loads the matching skill.
go.use_bearing_when: The go-api stack (pgx, sqlc, goose, slog), the layout, the scaffold, CI and the make check gate, and every conflict with the pack.

llm-guardrails.why: gstack /cso audits LLM security as one of its phases (user input reaching system prompts, unbounded LLM spend) and verifies findings, but it builds nothing. llm-guardrails builds the policy file, the input, tool-tier and output checks in one module wired at the gateway, and a parametrised adversarial fixture suite whose passing count must equal the fixture count and which fails on zero fixtures. Its --audit mode is narrower than /cso but checks wiring /cso does not (call sites without check_input, tools without a tier). Measured 25 Sep 2026: a tie, 0.79 for the skill, /cso and no skill. The skill lost on taking a side-effect target from document content, putting other people's derived records in the prompt, and not testing over-blocking or reply text; those four were added to the skill the same day. A rerun is owed before a verdict.
llm-guardrails.use_alternative_when: Finding LLM security holes in existing code as part of a wider security audit.
llm-guardrails.use_bearing_when: Adding guardrails to an LLM feature and proving they catch the adversarial set.

session-handoff.why: For per-branch work session-handoff is stronger because the Bearing SessionStart hook prints the state file back automatically and the Gate line is computed from the .check-passed marker, so the next session sees whether the gate is stale without invoking anything. gsd-pause-work is stronger for multi-session plans: it writes machine-readable HANDOFF.json, measures uncommitted files from git rather than memory, records blocking constraints the resume step enforces, and commits the handoff. context-save only writes to ~/.gstack and needs a manual /context-restore; mattpocock handoff writes to the OS temp dir.
session-handoff.use_alternative_when: The work is a GSD phase or spans many sessions with a plan, decisions and blocking constraints that must gate resumption.
session-handoff.use_bearing_when: Pausing a single task branch in a work repository before /clear or end of day.

harness-setup.why: No installed skill makes a repository work with Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot, OpenCode, Windsurf, Cline, Zed or Kiro. harness-setup runs bin/brg-harness, which writes each harness's thin adapters over the shared bin/brg-guard, fails closed when the event JSON cannot be read, and never overwrites a differing file (it writes <file>.bearing-new and counts conflicts). The kit's named alternative is a manual npx skills add, which installs skills but no rules or guard hooks. GSD's installer targets many runtimes but only for GSD's own files.
harness-setup.use_bearing_when: A repository or engineer needs the standard and its guard rails in a non-Claude harness.

health-checks.why: canary is a time-boxed browser watch after a deploy (screenshots, console errors, load time against a baseline) that produces a one-off report. health-checks builds standing mechanisms: /healthz and /readyz with named concurrent dependency checks, a scheduled synthetic suite in CI, blackbox probes and flap alerts with runbooks. No installed skill builds readiness endpoints or synthetic journeys.
health-checks.use_alternative_when: Watching a web app for ten minutes right after a deploy.
health-checks.use_bearing_when: Adding health endpoints, synthetic checks and uptime alerting to a service.

high-level-design.why: Confirmed with nuance. As an author high-level-design is stronger: goal and non-goals must be agreed before section 2, failure-mode cells that nobody can fill are written UNDEFINED, the scaling section needs a number, and every claim is sourced or prefixed 'assumption:'. /plan-eng-review does not write an HLD; it reviews one, with a scope challenge, one AskUserQuestion per issue, a failure-mode critical-gap rule and a default-on outside voice (Codex), which is a stronger review loop than Bearing's optional critic. Use Bearing to write, then /plan-eng-review on the result.
high-level-design.use_alternative_when: An HLD or plan already exists and needs an adversarial review before build.
high-level-design.use_bearing_when: The HLD document itself has to be written from a PRD and the code.

i18n.why: harden treats i18n as one line of a nine-item UI hardening matrix (no hard-coded strings, 1.3x expansion, RTL icon flip) and explicitly refuses counts. i18n counts hard-coded strings before and after, sets up the catalog per platform with ICU plurals and Intl formatters, a locale fallback chain, a pseudo-locale RTL pass, and an i18n-check that fails on zero keys compared or any missing key.
i18n.use_alternative_when: A general UI production-readiness pass where i18n is one of many states to check.
i18n.use_bearing_when: Actually internationalising a client or adding a locale.

incident.why: Nothing installed runs a live incident. internal-comms (Anthropic) lists incident reports but ships only generic comms guidelines (3P, newsletter, FAQ, general); investigate and gsd-debug do root-cause debugging, not severity, roles, UTC timeline and comms cadence. incident is scribe-only by design and never runs a remediation.
incident.use_alternative_when: investigate (gstack) in parallel for the root-cause hunt while incident keeps the record.
incident.use_bearing_when: Declaring, updating, communicating and resolving an incident.

infra.why: HashiCorp's three skills are narrow: a generic AWS-flavoured style guide, a thorough terraform test reference, and a module refactor recipe that ends in terraform apply. None covers remote state, environments, IAM breadth, secrets, Kubernetes, alerts, plan-only CI or the never-apply rule. terraform-test and terraform-refactor-module are stronger than infra on their own jobs, since infra had no test guidance and no moved blocks. infra now loads them for those jobs, limits tests to plan mode with mocks, and ends a refactor at a reviewed plan. Their correct rules (moved, import and removed blocks, output descriptions, underscore identifiers) were added to the guidelines.
infra.use_alternative_when: Writing .tftest.hcl files, splitting a root into modules, or HCL layout questions; infra loads them.
infra.use_bearing_when: Any Terraform, kustomize or monitoring change, review or infra scaffold, and whenever a pack skill suggests apply.

ios.why: swiftui-pro is a SwiftUI reviewer and is stronger than the lane's checklist at SwiftUI itself: deprecated against modern API, view extraction, performance, HIG and VoiceOver detail, across nine reference files. It agrees with the lane on @Observable @MainActor, .task and no GCD. It has no scaffold, gate, Keychain, XcodeGen, privacy manifest or Swift 6 migration guidance, and assumes iOS 26 where the lane's floor is iOS 17. The lane therefore loads it for SwiftUI view writing and review and keeps everything else. /ios-qa (gstack) remains the choice for device QA.
ios.use_alternative_when: Writing or reviewing SwiftUI views for API modernity, composition, performance and accessibility detail; /ios-qa for a running app on a device.
ios.use_bearing_when: Swift and SwiftUI conventions, review against project rules, scaffolding, and the gate; it calls swiftui-pro itself.

background-jobs.why: No installed skill builds background jobs generically (the Cloudflare queue references are platform-specific). background-jobs writes a per-job contract that stops on an empty idempotency key, fixes backoff with full jitter, visibility above timeout, SIGTERM redelivery and dead letters, and requires five property tests. Handlers claim the idempotency key with an insert guarded by a unique constraint in the same transaction as the side effect, and a unique violation means done or in progress, the atomic pattern api-and-interface-design requires.
background-jobs.use_bearing_when: Any queue, cron or outbox job needs its failure contract, worker shutdown, metrics and tests.

low-level-design.why: low-level-design counts the design gaps: sequences without an error branch are written UNDEFINED, each query must name its index, config vars are checked against .env.example, and any work item over 400 lines is split before writing. writing-plans produces executable TDD steps with exact code, a no-placeholder rule and a reviewer-subagent prompt, which is stronger for execution but carries no queries, indexes, transactions or error mapping. They chain: low-level-design's work breakdown feeds writing-plans.
low-level-design.use_alternative_when: The design is settled and the next step is bite-sized TDD tasks with exact code for an executor.
low-level-design.use_bearing_when: One HLD component needs its modules, queries, transactions, errors and config designed before tasks are cut.

llm-eval.why: Read in full with gsd-eval-auditor and gsd-eval-planner, the GSD pair plans eval dimensions and later audits whether they were implemented, scored by a deterministic eval.score verb with an adversarial auditor stance. It never builds anything: no golden set, no graders, no harness, no baseline, no CI gate, and it only runs inside a GSD phase that has a SUMMARY.md. llm-eval builds all of those, tests every grader with an oracle and a null case, fails on zero cases, and gates on a delta against a person-accepted baseline. GSD's advice of 10 to 20 examples is also looser than Bearing's minimums.
llm-eval.use_alternative_when: Auditing, after a GSD phase, whether the planned eval dimensions and guardrails were actually implemented.
llm-eval.use_bearing_when: Building or running the eval for any LLM feature; a coverage audit like GSD's could be added as a llm-eval --audit mode.

llm-gateway.why: Cloudflare AI Gateway is a hosted proxy configured on Cloudflare with caching, rate limits and fallbacks, documented for Vercel AI SDK and OpenAI SDK patterns. llm-gateway builds an in-code module: routing by tier, idempotency keys, per-tenant limits, cost from response usage, gen_ai spans, a kill switch, tests on a recorded-response fake, and a gate that call sites outside llm/ must reach zero. The hosted product could be a provider behind Bearing's module, not a replacement for it.
llm-gateway.use_alternative_when: The service runs on Cloudflare and wants provider analytics and caching at the edge; put it behind the Bearing module as the transport.
llm-gateway.use_bearing_when: Any service that calls a model.

llm-fine-tuning.why: Read on 25 Sep 2026: huggingface-llm-trainer writes and submits runnable TRL and PEFT jobs to Hugging Face Jobs (SFT, DPO, GRPO, Unsloth) and is stronger for the run itself; trl-training covers the TRL command line on any machine. Neither decides whether to train against an eval, gates on a smoke run, serves the adapter with vLLM behind the product's gateway or writes the model card. llm-fine-tuning now does those and routes the run to them. Measured 25 Sep 2026 against no skill (huggingface-llm-trainer is not installed): 0.96 against 0.70.
llm-fine-tuning.use_alternative_when: Running the training job on Hugging Face Jobs (huggingface-llm-trainer) or with the TRL CLI (trl-training).
llm-fine-tuning.use_bearing_when: Deciding whether to train, preparing the data, the GPU check and smoke run, serving behind the gateway, the canary and the model card.

load-test.why: Grafana's k6 skill is the stronger script author: protocol examples for HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket and browser, a docs lookup through k6 x docs, a validate loop that runs or inspects the script, and a best-practices review. It does not derive thresholds from the HLD SLOs, has no production refusal, writes to k6/scripts/, adds no make target, CI job or results table, and suggests k6 cloud run, which the settings template denies. load-test now loads it for writing and checking the script and keeps target resolution, the production-host refusal, SLO-derived thresholds with abortOnFail, the four stages, teardown, make load-test failing on zero scripts, the manual qa-only CI job and the per-commit results table.
load-test.use_alternative_when: Writing or debugging a one-off k6 script outside the SLO workflow: a gRPC, WebSocket or browser scenario, choosing an executor, or looking up a k6 API.
load-test.use_bearing_when: Any load, stress or soak test of a service in a repository on this standard; it calls k6 itself when installed.

logging.why: addyosmani gives the principles (structured events, correlation id, levels, never log secrets) with Express snippets but no inventory, no templates and no gate. logging counts boundaries before and after, lists stray print calls, binds the request id at the edge, ships HTTP logging templates for six stacks behind LOG_HTTP toggles, and runs the repo gate. addyosmani has two rules Bearing lacks: a stable event name field on every line and an entryPoint field when several entry points (scheduler, replay, CLI) write one sink; its 'spot-check actual output for PII' is also stronger than Bearing's static deny list.
logging.use_alternative_when: Reviewing a PR for telemetry quality or teaching the why; stacks Bearing has no template for (Node/Express).
logging.use_bearing_when: Establishing or repairing logging in a repo on the Bearing stacks, with counts and HTTP logging toggles.

mcp-server.why: The prior finding partly holds: build-mcp-server is the stronger designer (remote HTTP versus MCPB versus stdio, search plus execute for large surfaces, elicitation, Claude connector review and directory submission) but it writes no tests and has no client mode. Both build a server, so this is not a different job; Bearing wins on mechanism with a protocol-level test per tool whose count must equal tools exposed, and a client that maps discovered tools into tiers with new tools irreversible. Every tool also sets a title and all four annotation hints from its tier, and the protocol test fails a tool without them. mcp-builder still ships an LLM evaluation script Bearing does not have.
mcp-server.use_alternative_when: Deciding deployment and distribution (remote connector, MCPB, directory submission) or wrapping a large API; mcp-builder for an LLM-driven eval of the finished server.
mcp-server.use_bearing_when: Building and testing a server or client inside a service repository; add tool annotations from build-mcp-server's tool-design reference.

db-migration.why: No installed skill scaffolds schema migrations with a lock and index header and an up, down, up proof. mattpocock migrate-to-shoehorn is a test-library migration and cloudflare-one-migrations is a SASE vendor migration; both only match the word. The skill's substance is the per-tool layout for nine tools and the migrate-verify target it creates when none exists. The packs added in round two do not change this: supabase-postgres-best-practices claims migrations but its only migration advice is idempotent DO blocks, and golang-database tells the agent to use golang-migrate and never write migration SQL.

app-store-release.why: gstack ship carries a real App Store adapter the kit lists as "none": fastlane end to end, a preflight for the 1024pt icon, privacy manifests and ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption, and an idempotency log that stops a re-upload on ambiguity. It is iOS only, executes uploads and submission itself, and mints a standing App Store Connect API key. app-store-release covers both stores, Android versionCode across every track, phased rollout with halt criteria and dashboards, Play Data safety from the SDK list, and a rejection playbook, while printing every command. It now also runs gstack's iOS preflight checks (1024 icon without alpha, privacy manifest, export compliance, usage strings) and keeps an upload log that blocks a repeat upload.
app-store-release.use_alternative_when: A solo iOS app where the owner wants the agent to archive, upload and submit through fastlane.
app-store-release.use_bearing_when: Any Play or App Store submission in a work repository, rollout planning, or a rejection reply.

motion-design.why: ui-craft animate, backed by the 434-line references/motion.md, has deeper web motion craft: a decision ladder, a reduced-motion contract, FLIP, and an audit for missing motion. It is web-only, edits code with no test, and reads durations from its own budget table. motion-design covers React Native, Compose and SwiftUI, reads durations from the tokens, and writes a Playwright test that asserts the final state and getAnimations().length === 0 under reduced motion. It also runs two counts that must hold: reduced-motion paths must equal patterns applied, and layout properties animated must be zero. Its own gotcha 'none installed does motion design' is stale, because animate is installed and listed in ALTERNATES.
motion-design.use_alternative_when: Tuning or trimming web motion by eye (easing, stagger, choreography), or when the job is removing motion that is too much.
motion-design.use_bearing_when: Motion must come from tokens, work on native stacks, and ship with a reduced-motion test and the counted gate.

merge-request.why: gstack /ship verifies more (coverage audit, pre-landing review army, adversarial review, evidence ledger) but it is a non-interactive pipeline that includes uncommitted changes, merges the base into the branch, squashes WIP commits, bumps VERSION on every PR and pushes; the kit's claim that it "stops at the push" is only true because bearing's block-publish hook blocks it, after the branch has already been mutated. merge-request prepares the description, audits commit subjects and trailers without rewriting history, stops on a zero-file diff, and prints the push and MR URL. For preparing an MR a human pushes, merge-request is stronger; ship's review and coverage steps are separate jobs covered by branch-review and definition-of-done.
merge-request.use_alternative_when: A solo repository where the agent is allowed to commit, merge base, version and open the PR end to end.
merge-request.use_bearing_when: Any work repository where the engineer pushes and opens the MR.

new-repo.why: No installed skill scaffolds a repository from stack templates. The closest, gsd-new-project, creates planning files (.planning/PROJECT.md, ROADMAP.md) and runs git init, but installs no Makefile, CI, hooks or agent files. brg-scaffold is a real script: it refuses a non-empty target, fails when zero files were written, and reports the count of unfilled placeholders, which must be 0.
new-repo.use_alternative_when: Use gsd-new-project for project planning (requirements, roadmap), which can run alongside new-repo.

nextjs.why: nextjs covers the full job: server-by-default boundary, the authorise then validate then act order for server actions, split env with server-only, cache named on every fetch, route states, testing server components, and a scaffold. Vercel adds server-side performance rules Bearing lacks (server-no-shared-module-state, server-serialization, after()), but no structure, security order or tests. The lane is on Next 16.3 with Cache Components: proxy.ts replaces middleware.ts, actions use updateTag, and it has taken in Vercel's rules on waterfalls, barrel imports, shared server module state and serialisation.
nextjs.use_alternative_when: Tuning server-render performance: parallel fetches, RSC payload size, per-request dedup, non-blocking after().
nextjs.use_bearing_when: Writing, reviewing or scaffolding a Next App Router app, especially server actions, env handling and tests. Upgrade the lane to Next 16 before new projects start on it.

node.why: No installed skill covers Node service code (workers-best-practices is Cloudflare Workers only). The lane gives what an unguided model would not do consistently: Fastify 5 with a Zod type provider on every route and the response, one error envelope, floating-promise lint, Drizzle repositories with services owning transactions, migrations never run on boot, OTel loaded before pg and pino, bounded shutdown, and a scaffold with pinned versions. Weakest spot: it targets Node 22 and pnpm 9 when Node 24 has been Active LTS since Oct 2025 and pnpm 10 is current.
node.use_alternative_when: The service runs on Cloudflare Workers: use workers-best-practices and wrangler instead.
node.use_bearing_when: Any Node or TypeScript server code on Fastify, Express or similar, and scaffolding node-api.

observability.why: otel-instrumentation is a far deeper reference (about 8,200 lines: per-SDK setup for ten languages, span/metric/log hygiene, a dependency verification rule and a post-deploy validation checklist) but it is advisory only: no collector or compose template, no dashboard, no alert rules, no SLO document, and 18 of its links point at otel-collector and otel-ottl skills that are not installed. observability ships templates, burn-rate rules, promtool check, and a gate that rule count must equal runbook count, plus a local trace-to-log join check. It now defines what working means and the on-call questions before instrumenting, test-fires each new alert, and samples in the collector rather than the SDK, so the RED metrics derived from spans stay whole. It still lacks otel-instrumentation's per-language span hygiene for stacks it does not cover.
observability.use_alternative_when: Instrumenting a stack Bearing does not cover (Java, .NET, Ruby, PHP, Scala, Next.js App Router) or needing span-kind/status/attribute hygiene and a backend validation checklist; addyosmani when deciding what to instrument for a new feature.
observability.use_bearing_when: Wiring a Go, Python, React or mobile service end to end with the collector, Grafana stack, RED dashboard, burn-rate alerts, SLO doc and runbook stubs.

on-call.why: No installed skill sets up rotations, escalation or error-budget policy; addyosmani only states alert rules (actionable, runbook, two severities). on-call's check mode fails on zero rules, a paging alert without a runbook file, or an unroutable rule, and prints counts. It lacks addyosmani's test-fire-each-alert rule, which belongs here or in observability.
on-call.use_bearing_when: Rotation, routing, error-budget freeze rule, handover and weekly page review.

feature-patterns.why: No installed skill covers these eight mechanisms generically; the Cloudflare skill has platform-specific rate-limit, queue and multitenancy references only. feature-patterns loads exactly one reference, greps its markers for existing implementations before asking, skips questions an ADR answers, and writes a plan with failure modes and named tests. Its payments reference derives the Idempotency-Key from the payment intent, reuses it across retries, and keeps it longer than the retry, dead-letter and dispute windows.
feature-patterns.use_bearing_when: Planning uploads, search, realtime, cache, rate limiting, payments, notifications or multitenancy.

performance.why: web-perf is a deeper browser page-load audit (DevTools trace insights, network chains, bundle analysis) but it stops unless the chrome-devtools MCP server is configured, and it is not configured in ~/.claude.json. performance covers backend and mobile profilers, refuses to touch code before a metric line exists, stops on zero measurements, and treats an after-median inside the before spread as noise to revert. gstack benchmark is page-level regression tracking.
performance.use_alternative_when: A web page's LCP, INP or CLS, once the chrome-devtools MCP is added.
performance.use_bearing_when: Any slow endpoint, job, memory growth or app startup.

postmortem.why: pm-skills retro is a sprint retrospective (Start/Stop/Continue, velocity versus commitment, two or three actions); gstack retro is a weekly shipping retro and mattpocock retro improves the agent's environment. None produces an incident record with impact numbers, a UTC timeline marking inferred times, a causal chain and owned follow-ups. The kit's own label for retro, 'the team half', is accurate.
postmortem.use_alternative_when: The team-process retro after a sprint, not an outage.

prd.why: prd extracts numbered REQ statements from an existing input, records the source line next to each, flags vague words as ambiguous with an open question, never renumbers existing ids, and treats zero statements extracted as a failed run. create-prd writes an eight-section business document from scratch (contacts, OKRs, value proposition, release) with no ids, no source tracing and no failure condition. mattpocock to-spec is further off: it writes an extensive numbered user-story list, which is the one-story-per-line pattern the owner rejects. gsd-ingest-docs normalises many documents into .planning/ with a conflict engine, but its requirements come from GSD scoping rather than line-level extraction.
prd.use_alternative_when: There is no input to normalise and stakeholders need a business case document with objectives, segments and value propositions.
prd.use_bearing_when: Any brief, email or old PRD must become the traceable root that stories, tests and commits cite.

privacy-review.why: cso Phase 11 is a fill-in classification block (restricted, confidential, internal, public) with no mechanisms. privacy-review builds the data map from the schema, wires retention and table-driven DSAR export and delete, designs append-only consent, scans every log call for PII and fails on zero calls scanned, and writes tests against a seeded subject. gsd-domain-researcher touches regulation only as research input.
privacy-review.use_alternative_when: A quick data sensitivity overview inside a security audit.
privacy-review.use_bearing_when: Any GDPR or DPDP work that must end in working retention, DSAR and consent.

client-handover.why: The handover-named skills (mattpocock handoff, gsd-pause-work, context-save) hand a session to another agent; gsd-onboard and document-generate onboard or document a codebase. None produces a client pack with an access inventory scanned for credential patterns, environments, licences, known debt with ticket keys and a sign-off page. It reads build targets from the Makefile with Read and Grep, as the doc-writer agent it runs under allows.
client-handover.use_alternative_when: Never for a client handover; mattpocock handoff for agent-to-agent session transfer.

prompt-registry.why: The two answer different halves. claude-api prompt-audit is clearly stronger at judging prompt text: pattern groups for dated instructions tied to the target model, provenance, a keep list, a per-hunk diff and a before and after behavioural probe. prompt-registry owns the lifecycle it lacks: a versioned registry with frontmatter, one loader that validates variables before the call, render tests that fail on zero prompts, and a score per version that keeps the old version active on a regression. Bearing's own audit mode only finds inline prompts, not bad prompt text.
prompt-registry.use_alternative_when: Improving or auditing the wording of prompts, skills or tool descriptions, and after every model migration.
prompt-registry.use_bearing_when: Putting prompts under version control with tests and per-version eval scores; call prompt-audit from its improve mode.

prose-lint.why: clarify is a 36-line lens that critiques UI labels, errors and empty states only. prose-lint covers docs, MR text, commits and comments, greps each pattern with a per-file hit count before editing, re-greps after, and carries rewrite rules for em dashes by what follows the dash. clarify is stronger on UX copy judgement (is the label clear), which is a different question from the AI-tell lint.
prose-lint.use_alternative_when: UI microcopy needs to be clearer or more specific, not just free of AI tells.
prose-lint.use_bearing_when: Docs, READMEs, MR descriptions, commits and comments before an MR.

python.why: gstack's review checklist has a few Python-specific lines (async/sync mixing, shell injection, parameterised SQL) but no conventions for writing FastAPI code. python gives concrete, correct guidance: pure ASGI middleware over BaseHTTPMiddleware, lazy='raise' on relationships, expire_on_commit=False, per-request AsyncSession, Alembic on the async engine, asgi-lifespan in tests, and a ruff rule set including ASYNC and DTZ. The lane is on Python 3.14.
python.use_alternative_when: A whole-branch review where Python is one language among several; gstack /review adds its cross-cutting checks.
python.use_bearing_when: Writing or reviewing FastAPI/SQLAlchemy code and scaffolding python-api.

rag.why: The only installed RAG-building material is Cloudflare's Vectorize and AI Search references, which build retrieval on Cloudflare's hosted products. rag builds on pgvector in the team's own Postgres with versioned idempotent ingestion, an embedding ADR, HNSW parameters stated, citations on every hit, and recall@5, recall@10 and MRR on a golden set that fails on zero questions. Nothing else installed measures retrieval.
rag.use_alternative_when: The system is deployed on Cloudflare Workers and a managed index is acceptable.
rag.use_bearing_when: RAG on the team stack (Postgres, pgvector) or any RAG that must be measured.

react.why: Vercel's skill is a 70-rule performance catalogue (waterfalls, bundle, re-renders) with no state model, validation, accessibility, testing, scaffold or gate. react covers the whole job for a Vite SPA: a server-state rule, Zod at every boundary, typed query keys, a four-state render rule, a 79-line review checklist and a scaffold with pinned versions and a fail-on-empty make check. It has taken in Vercel's waterfall and barrel-import rules. Two Vercel rules still do not fit this stack: client-swr-dedup (Bearing uses TanStack Query) and rerender-memo (Bearing bans unmeasured memo).
react.use_alternative_when: A measured performance problem (bundle size, waterfalls, re-render storms, long lists) needs a specific fix. Skip its SWR rule in TanStack Query repos.
react.use_bearing_when: Writing, reviewing or scaffolding any React web code: state, data fetching, validation, a11y, tests and the gate.

react-native.why: The Expo skills know the current SDK better than the lane: expo-router covers native stack headers, form sheets, NativeTabs, link previews and the SDK 56+ expo-router/react-navigation import rule, and expo-upgrade holds the SDK bump procedure and the deprecation table (it flagged the lane's AsyncStorage default, now replaced by expo-sqlite/localStorage). Neither gives state ownership (TanStack Query versus Zustand), Zod at boundaries, secure-store rules, list and accessibility rules, a scaffold or a gate. expo-dev-client, eas-update and eas-app-stores are not installed: they run EAS cloud builds or publish, which the repo settings deny. The lane's Expo 57.0.24 pin clears expo-upgrade's 57.0.9 Hermes V1 floor.
react-native.use_alternative_when: An Expo SDK bump or a deprecated package (expo-upgrade); native navigation UI and router import paths (expo-router).
react-native.use_bearing_when: Any Expo or React Native code, review or scaffold on this stack; it calls both skills itself.

refactor.why: improve-codebase-architecture chooses what to restructure (deepening candidates, an HTML report, a grilling loop, CONTEXT.md and ADR updates) and explicitly stops before proposing interfaces. refactor executes a chosen restructuring safely: green baseline or stop, characterisation tests when none exist, one mechanical transform per commit with check and tests between, a diff ceiling, and a behaviour gate that undoes any step touching a test, fixture, public signature or user string. The outputs serve different stages, so they chain rather than compete.
refactor.use_alternative_when: Deciding which modules to deepen and designing the target shape.
refactor.use_bearing_when: Carrying out the restructuring once the target is chosen.
