release.why: release-notes turns tickets into user-facing prose and touches no version, tag or file. gstack ship's Step 12 has a tested version-bump CLI but bumps per PR in a 4-digit scheme and never tags. release derives semver from Conventional Commits since the last tag, stops on zero commits, edits exactly the version fields across seven stack files (including Android versionCode and iOS build number), runs the gate and prints the tag and push commands. With --package (the former publish skill) it also derives semver from the exported-surface diff (gorelease, apidiff, griffe or .d.ts), stops on zero exported symbols, inspects the tarball with npm pack --dry-run, checks the README install name, orders workspace publishes topologically and states provenance honestly; no installed skill does API-diff semver or a pack check.
release.use_alternative_when: Writing the customer-facing announcement from the CHANGELOG release produced.
release.use_bearing_when: Cutting a tagged release of a service or app, or with --package a library, SDK or CLI.

task-report.why: task-report is a per-task outcome report where Verified may cite only commands run this session with their output, and anything not run goes under Not done as "not run". The GSD session report is a stakeholder summary driven by .planning/STATE.md, git log over 24 hours and estimated token usage, so it does not bind claims to executed commands. No installed skill produces the Changed / Verified / Not done / Noticed shape; the gstack completion protocol (DONE, BLOCKED) is a status line, not a report.
task-report.use_alternative_when: A GSD milestone needs a session summary for stakeholders with phase progress.
task-report.use_bearing_when: Closing any task; it is the owner's mandated report shape.

resilience-testing.why: No installed skill plans fault injection, restore drills or DR tests; chaos appears only as a mention in gstack plan-eng-review. resilience-testing turns the HLD failure-mode table into faults with expected behaviour, abort and revert commands, stops on zero failure modes, records measured RTO and RPO against claims, and never injects a fault itself.
resilience-testing.use_bearing_when: Any chaos, backup restore or DR question.

branch-review.why: branch-review now runs gstack /review as its engine, so it inherits everything the alternative finds, then adds two mechanisms /review lacks: the stack checklists applied item by item with a 'checked, none found' line each, and one fresh-context verifier per Critical and High that sees only path, claim and failure scenario. gstack's own adversarial pass and pre-emit gate hunt for new findings or self-check quotes; neither is an independent confirm or refute of each finding. It also stops on a zero-file diff and fixes the /review auto-fix risk by passing 'ask before any fix'.
branch-review.use_alternative_when: A quick self-review of your own branch where independent verification is not worth the extra agents, or a repository not set up with Bearing.
branch-review.use_bearing_when: Any MR on the standard, or a review that must not touch the tree (--engine bearing).

runbook.why: The kit's named alternate, document-generate (gstack), is a Diataxis writer with no runbook shape at all; addyosmani's runbook section is the closer match but is a three-line minimum and guidance. runbook finds the alert rule by name, fills eight sections with copy-pasteable commands and healthy-versus-unhealthy results, flags a missing runbook_url, and counts placeholders. It writes "Last verified: not run" unless the diagnosis commands actually ran. addyosmani's rule to update the runbook when closing each incident is still absent.
runbook.use_alternative_when: A three-line stub while writing alerts in a repo off this standard.
runbook.use_bearing_when: Any runbook for a named alert.

screen-design.why: design-html turns one approved mockup into Pretext HTML for production, checked with screenshots at three widths. It has no state switching, no inventory of states and no dark-theme check. ui-craft craft builds the real surface in the app and treats states as build steps, but it produces code, not a prototype to build from. screen-design adds two gates that run as scripts. states_check.py fails when any state in the inventory has no reachable panel or a placeholder is unfilled, and also fails when zero screens were checked. evidence.py fails when a width is missing or the dark theme did not apply. Neither alternative verifies either property.
screen-design.use_alternative_when: Use design-html to finalise one approved screen into production HTML with text layout that really reflows. Use craft or sddesign to build the surface straight in the codebase and skip the prototype.
screen-design.use_bearing_when: Developers (web or native) need a standalone prototype per screen with every state switchable, redlines, component names and event names.

secrets.why: cso finds secrets with git log prefix greps and reports them; it stops there. secrets owns what follows: an inventory with owners and rotation dates, rotation per type with dual-read, the ordered leak response (revoke, rotate, scrub, blast radius count, notify) with a record, gitleaks with a pre-commit hook, and env-parity.sh that exits non-zero on zero variables read. Its scripts/ci-credentials.py adds cso's check for inline credentials in CI files, without printing any value.
secrets.use_alternative_when: Broad security sweep to discover secrets alongside other findings.
secrets.use_bearing_when: Inventory, rotation, leak response, scanning setup and .env parity.

new-skill.why: skill-creator is the stronger engine: run_eval.py, aggregate_benchmark.py, grader and analyzer agents, a review viewer and a description optimiser, run with and without the skill. new-skill does not replace it but calls it in step 7 with a fixed brief, then adds gates skill-creator lacks for this kit: claude plugin validate --strict, make lint-skills and lint-tools, and lint-evals, which fails a new skill with no evals.json, plus the rule that a skill which does not beat the baseline is not added. For creating a Bearing skill it is therefore a superset. Superpowers writing-skills (pressure-test RED-GREEN) is the better guide for rule-enforcing discipline skills outside the kit.
new-skill.use_alternative_when: The skill being written is not a Bearing skill in the Bearing checkout.
new-skill.use_bearing_when: Adding a skill to Bearing, where the house lints, registry rows and the eval gate must pass.

spike.why: The job is a timeboxed investigation, and spike is the only one with a clock: a written start time, a stop condition set before code, a 50 percent check that asks continue or stop, a hard stop at 100 percent, and a git status check that reverts any change outside the scratch location. gsd-spike is deeper as exploration (Given/When/Then decomposition into several spikes, prior-spike reading, a forensic observability layer, frontier mode, wrap-up into a findings skill), but it states depth over speed and has no timebox or production-file guard. Both rely on the model following written steps; neither ships a script for these checks.
spike.use_alternative_when: A new product idea needs several feasibility questions explored in depth, with no fixed time budget, inside a GSD project.
spike.use_bearing_when: One yes, no or numeric question must be answered within a fixed number of hours in a product repository without touching production files.

best_alternative.name: user-stories
best_alternative.note: to-tickets is stronger but user-invocable only, so it cannot run in an unattended eval arm

backlog.why: backlog ships scripts/coverage_check.py, which computes coverage from the AC Covers: lines in the files rather than from the model's matrix and exits 1 on an uncovered REQ, an unknown or withdrawn REQ, an epic with no journey, or zero REQ or zero stories read. It also judges each statement (seed, criterion, variant, duplicate, split) before writing stories. to-tickets has good vertical-slice and blocking-edge rules and a user quiz, but no link back to requirement ids and no coverage check; pm-skills user-stories is a template with INVEST guidance and nothing that verifies. GSD's roadmapper demands 100 percent requirement coverage, but only to phases and only as model-judged prose.
backlog.use_alternative_when: A spec or conversation needs cutting into agent-sized tracer-bullet tickets with blocking edges and there is no numbered PRD to trace.
backlog.use_bearing_when: A numbered PRD exists and every REQ must be provably covered by an acceptance criterion.

start-task.why: start-task refuses a dirty tree, picks the base by branch type (develop for feature, main for hotfix), validates the task id shape, names the branch type/ID-PascalName and writes a state file with the acceptance criteria that session-handoff, definition-of-done and merge-request later read. using-git-worktrees only isolates a workspace and runs setup plus baseline tests; it has no id, base-selection or criteria record. The one thing worktrees adds that start-task lacks is the green baseline test run before work starts.
start-task.use_alternative_when: Work must run in an isolated worktree beside the main checkout; run it after start-task has named the branch.
start-task.use_bearing_when: Starting any ticketed task in a work repository: branch name, base and criteria record.

test-automation.why: Against ai-test-generation, unchanged: its hallucination gate is a grep plus tsc and a human keep-or-reject per test, where test-automation builds the suite on six stacks with ref_check.py and a make target that fails on zero files. property-based-testing does a different job and is stronger at it (alternative-stronger for property design): a property catalog with a strength order, generators constrained in the strategy rather than assume(), tautology and vacuity traps, the repository's existing library, and a classification of shrunk failures. It builds no suite, applies no TC naming and runs no reference gate. test-automation loads it for inv: rows and for parser, codec, normalizer, validator, comparator and money rows, passes the property and generator to test-writer, and asks before adding a library.
test-automation.use_alternative_when: Writing, reviewing or debugging property tests outside the TC table, or classifying a shrunk counterexample.
test-automation.use_bearing_when: Turning planned TC rows into named tests on any supported stack; it calls property-based-testing itself for property rows.

test-cases.why: ai-test-generation has the deeper analysis: explicit versus inferred requirements, a risk table, an ambiguity list that must be resolved, and concurrency and state-transition categories. test-cases has the mechanism: cases_check.py reads the backlog and the table, fails on an uncovered AC, a duplicate id, a row with no or vague oracle and a P1 row without a not: check, and exits 1 on zero criteria or zero rows. It also keeps stable TC ids that automation and traceability depend on. test-scenarios (pm-skills) is a template with no gate.
test-cases.use_alternative_when: The source is a raw PRD or OpenAPI spec with unresolved ambiguities; run its risk and ambiguity steps first.
test-cases.use_bearing_when: Producing the persistent TC table from a backlog in a work repository.

test-heal.why: The two share the 20-run reproduce and 50/50 proof bar, and test-reliability adds confidence scoring, an intent-fidelity rollback and time-sensitivity and visual flake classes. test-heal is stronger on not hiding regressions: regression is a first-class class that is never edited, weakening an assertion is named as hiding a regression, every heal is followed by a whole-suite re-run that reverts a heal causing new failures, it exits non-zero on zero failures, and it has repeat commands for five runners instead of Playwright only. playwright-cli's heal confirms with a single rerun and lists "assertion text updated in the app" as a fixable cause; selector-drift-recovery's score-candidates.mjs exits 0 on zero applied candidates.
test-heal.use_alternative_when: Building confidence-scored runtime healing into a Playwright suite, or bulk selector regeneration after a planned redesign (selector-drift-recovery).
test-heal.use_bearing_when: Triage and repair of failures from a test-run report.

test-run.why: gstack qa-only explores a running web app like a user and reports bugs with screenshots; it does not run the repository's suites. test-run inventories every suite, runs each through its machine-readable reporter, sums real test events (a Go package with no test files is zero, not a pass), marks a missing runner or timeout as not run with a non-zero exit, and writes a dated md plus json report with TC and story ids. No installed skill parses suite output this way.
test-run.use_alternative_when: Exploratory QA of a deployed or local web app beyond the written tests.
test-run.use_bearing_when: Running the automated suites and producing the evidence report for a commit.

themes.why: theme-lint.py is a real gate. It resolves every role in every theme, computes WCAG contrast from oklch for each pair, checks hex drift, and exits 1 when zero themes are found. It also writes the preview. ui-craft tokens and themes.md offer the intentional-dark test and four presets whose contrast is verified by hand with APCA. They have no runtime switching, no tenant validation and no script. theme-factory is for slide decks.
themes.use_alternative_when: Picking a starting preset or accent family for a web surface with no brand (ui-craft themes.md), or a slide-deck theme (theme-factory).
themes.use_bearing_when: Adding dark, high-contrast, brand, tenant or seasonal themes to a product, with contrast gated in make check and switching on each stack.

threat-model.why: security-threat-model has the stronger analysis (alternative-stronger for that step): attacker capabilities with written non-capabilities, multi-step abuse paths tied to assets, every claim anchored in repository evidence, and an assumption check with the user before ranking. It needs code, uses TM ids that nothing downstream reads, maps no mitigation to a story and has no gate. threat-model runs it as the abuse-path pass in step 4 when code exists, then writes stable T-nn rows under STRIDE with mitigations as file:line, a story or a new story, and threats_check.py fails a sensitive scope with zero threats. It also works on a design with no code, and vapt-report cites its ids. gsd-secure-phase remains the choice inside GSD phases.
threat-model.use_alternative_when: A one-off AppSec threat model of an existing codebase that feeds no backlog and no VAPT report.
threat-model.use_bearing_when: Any threat model that must feed stories and vapt-report, and any design-time model before code; it calls the pack itself when code exists.

traceability.why: gsd-audit-milestone does a strong three-source requirement coverage check with orphan detection, but only over GSD's own .planning artifacts (REQUIREMENTS.md, VERIFICATION.md, SUMMARY frontmatter) and stops at 'requirement verified'. traceability walks the full chain REQ, story, AC, TC, test, commit, ticket, ADR, runbook and event with exact id patterns, names each gap class with its fixing skill, and treats a missing source as a counted gap instead of a stop. In a repository not run on GSD the alternative has nothing to read.
traceability.use_alternative_when: The project is run on GSD phases and you are closing a milestone.
traceability.use_bearing_when: Release sign-off or 'what has no tests' in a repository on the Bearing standard.

best_alternative.name: user-stories
best_alternative.note: to-tickets is stronger but user-invocable only, so it cannot run in an unattended eval arm

tracker-sync.why: tracker-sync runs every call through bin/brg-tracker, one command surface with fixed exit codes dispatching to real adapters for Jira, GitLab, GitHub and any REST tracker, keeps credentials out of the conversation, makes sync idempotent by writing Ticket: keys back into the backlog, and adds trace (branch, MR, commits, TC ids, ADR ids). to-tickets publishes via gh or glab as configured by setup-matt-pocock-skills, treats Jira and Linear as freeform prose, and has no generic REST adapter, no update, no trace and no idempotency. Its strength is deciding the slices, which is upstream of the tracker job.
tracker-sync.use_alternative_when: A GitHub or GitLab project with no Bearing configuration wants a spec sliced and filed as blocking-linked issues.
tracker-sync.use_bearing_when: Tickets live in Jira, a configured GitLab or GitHub, or a REST tracker and must be synced, updated and traced to MRs.

upgrade-tools.why: upgrade-tools is the only skill that updates every source (marketplace plugins, gstack, skills-CLI packs, GSD) with before and after versions, a count, and a doctor rerun, and it refuses to pull a dirty checkout. It upgrades gstack and GSD through their own upgraders (gstack-upgrade, gsd-update), which detect vendored installs and back up and restore local changes.
upgrade-tools.use_alternative_when: Only gstack or only GSD needs upgrading, or either has a vendored install or local patches to preserve.
upgrade-tools.use_bearing_when: The whole machine needs one pass across all sources with a version table and a doctor check.

ux-flows.why: plan-design-review's Passes 2, 3 and 7 are the source of ux-flows' state table, storyboard and 'engineer ships No items found' decision table. It works by amending a plan through one question per gap, and can add mockups. It has no screen inventory mapped to story ids, no navigation map keyed by screen id, no count of dead ends (screens with no way forward or back) that must reach zero, and no control inventory with target sizes, keyboard path and event names. ui-craft shape covers one screen, and customer-journey-map covers the marketing funnel from awareness to advocacy. Neither produces a flow package. The dead-end check is judged by the model, not a script.
ux-flows.use_alternative_when: A plan document already exists and needs its design gaps found and decided interactively, with mockups when an OpenAI key is set.
ux-flows.use_bearing_when: A feature needs its full screen set, per-screen states with copy, navigation and a dead-end-free flow before any variant or screen design.

vapt-report.why: The scanners find and vapt-report writes the commit-pinned position with threat-model links and a release decision. insecure-defaults:audit is a new finder, not a rival: six category sweeps then refuting verifiers trace each fallback secret, default credential, fail-open switch, weak crypto, permissive access and debug-leak candidate to its sink and to whether the deployment manifests supply the value, and it refuses a clean result when nothing was scanned. vapt-report now runs it in step 2 over the whole repository and keeps its counts on a separate line from the collector's.
vapt-report.use_alternative_when: Finding vulnerabilities at all: claude-security for depth, /cso for speed, and insecure-defaults:audit on its own for a configuration hardening pass outside a release.
vapt-report.use_bearing_when: A release needs a written, commit-pinned security position with threat-model links and a release decision.

webhooks.why: /cso Phase 6 only greps webhook routes for any signature verification and flags those without. webhooks builds both directions: raw-body HMAC with a constant-time compare, a 5 minute replay window, a unique (provider, event_id) row so duplicates ack without work, ack under 1 s, dual secrets during rotation, an outbound retry schedule with dead letter, a consumer-visible delivery log, and twelve TC-WH test cases.
webhooks.use_alternative_when: A quick security sweep for unsigned webhook endpoints across a repository.
webhooks.use_bearing_when: Building or hardening an inbound or outbound webhook integration.

workflow.why: workflow places the repository, branch, diff and gate result on one map spanning Bearing, Superpowers, gstack and GSD, and names the next skill whichever pack owns it. gsd-next is stronger mechanically, because it reads state through a script (gsd-tools smart-entry --json) and has hard invariants such as resuming a half-executed phase, but it only routes to GSD commands inside a .planning/ project. ui-craft start routes only within ui-craft and the gstack router only within gstack. workflow's detection is written steps with no script.
workflow.use_alternative_when: The work is already a GSD project with .planning/ state and the next step is a GSD phase command.
workflow.use_bearing_when: Someone asks what to do next or which skill to use in a company repository, across all packs.

autopilot.why: autopilot chains the Bearing stages from one statement to a prepared merge request, with every gate checked on disk by bin/brg-autopilot (a stage the model claims but the disk does not show is not done), every decision taken on the user's behalf written Proposed into one digest, and a hard stop before any push. gsd-autonomous runs planned GSD phases unattended and is stronger once a .planning/ roadmap exists, but it starts from a roadmap, not a statement, and has no decision digest or merge-request stop. Judged by reading; the end-to-end eval is the measurement.
autopilot.use_alternative_when: The work is already a GSD project with a roadmap and the phases only need executing.
autopilot.use_bearing_when: One requirement statement should become a reviewed merge request with nobody answering questions, and every decision taken must be reviewable afterwards.

docs-drift.why: gstack /document-release updates the docs a shipped diff touched, reading the diff. docs-drift answers a different question across the whole repository: which docs no longer match the code, whoever changed it and with whatever harness. Its script checks every path, make target and config name the docs mention and flags docs whose code moved on after them, prints counts, and fails on a broken reference or on zero docs; each finding goes to the side that is wrong, never a silent doc rewrite. Judged by reading; no eval has run.
docs-drift.use_alternative_when: A release just shipped and the docs it touched need the new behaviour.
docs-drift.use_bearing_when: Inheriting a codebase, before definition-of-done passes, or whenever a doc may have gone stale behind a manual or other-harness change.

verify-deploy.why: gstack /canary watches a deployed URL over a window for console errors, performance and page failures. verify-deploy is the ordered check right after a deploy, against the committed docs/environments.md: readiness, health, the deployed version matched to the tag or commit the engineer shipped, and smoke checks, GET only, with a report under docs/releases/ and a verdict; it never deploys or rolls back. Run it first, then /canary on prod. Judged by reading; no eval has run.
verify-deploy.use_alternative_when: Watching production for regressions over the minutes after a release.
verify-deploy.use_bearing_when: Proving the build you meant is the one serving, and that it is ready, right after a deploy to any environment.

speech.why: Read on 25 Sep 2026: Twilio's skills cover the phone leg of a voice agent (ConversationRelay message types, its interrupt event, streaming replies) on a Twilio account with Twilio's own speech engines. None covers engine choice by WER on the product's audio, diarisation, VAD and endpointing, a per-stage latency budget, or Indian and code-mixed languages, which speech measures with wer.py and latency_report.py. Measured 25 Sep 2026 against no skill (the Twilio skill is not installed): 0.96 against 0.88; the difference was reporting p95 latency against the budget and excluding broken turns.
speech.use_alternative_when: The calls go over Twilio: use it for the telephony leg and keep speech for measurement.
speech.use_bearing_when: Choosing and measuring a speech engine, building batch transcription or a real-time voice loop, setting the latency budget.

computer-vision.why: Read on 25 Sep 2026: huggingface-vision-trainer runs detector, classifier and SAM training on Hugging Face Jobs (paid plan) with mAP and accuracy; fiftyone-model-evaluation and fiftyone-dataset-curation do mAP, error browsing and curation inside FiftyOne. None covers few-shot anomaly detection, AUROC, a threshold chosen from the cost of a miss, group-safe splits, the VLM versus trained-model choice, or export and serving latency. Measured 25 Sep 2026 against no skill (the alternatives are not installed): 0.95 against 0.87; the difference was choosing the threshold on a held-out split and scoring test once.
computer-vision.use_alternative_when: Training on Hugging Face Jobs, or error analysis and curation in FiftyOne.
computer-vision.use_bearing_when: Choosing the approach, splitting by group, setting the operating threshold from costs, and shipping with latency measured.

tabular-ml.why: Searched the official marketplace and the huggingface, fiftyone and twilio skill repositories on 25 Sep 2026: nothing covers tabular or time-series ML (leakage-safe splits, a baseline gate, calibration, SHAP, drift). Platform plugins (sagemaker-ai, datarobot, databricks, dominodatalab) run jobs on their own platforms rather than teach the method. Measured 25 Sep 2026: 0.96 against 0.75 without a skill on two cases (leaky churn features with a rule baseline; seasonal alerting through a festival spike).
tabular-ml.use_alternative_when: The team already trains on one of those platforms: use its plugin for the job and keep tabular-ml's split and baseline gates.
tabular-ml.use_bearing_when: Any churn, scoring, forecasting or metric anomaly model.

defaultFiles.title: Your machine
defaultFiles.summary: Once per developer, outside every repository. install.sh writes them; nothing here is committed anywhere.

# <Your name>, <role> at <your company>

Personal notes for Claude Code on this machine. Kept short; every line is
loaded into every session.

## How I work

- Work repositories carry `AGENTS.md` and the Bearing skills. When unsure
  which step comes next, run `workflow`.
- One task per session. `start-task` to start, `session-handoff` to pause,
  `definition-of-done` then `merge-request` to finish.
- I push, merge and deploy. You prepare and print the command.

## Standing rules

- No em dashes in anything you write for me. Rewrite the sentence.
- No AI attribution in commits, MRs or documents.
- Report in the AGENTS.md shape: Changed, Verified, Not done, Noticed.
- If you did not run it, say "not run". Never claim a check you skipped.
- Ask one specific question when a request is ambiguous; otherwise proceed.

## Which skill

- Use the strongest skill for each step, whichever pack it comes from
  (Bearing, Superpowers, gstack, GSD Core, official plugins). A Bearing
  skill is used only where nothing installed does the step better; the
  handbook's skill pages show each comparison.
- When unsure which skill fits, run `workflow` or open the flow for
  the task (greenfield, bug fix, feature addition) in the handbook.
- Never on work repositories: cookie import, cross-model skills, deploy
  skills. The repository settings deny them.

# Bearing user configuration. Mode 600. Never inside a repository.
#
# Lives at ~/.config/bearing/bearing.env (XDG_CONFIG_HOME respected). The
# installer writes this file with placeholders; edit the values by hand.
# Format: KEY=value, one per line. A value with spaces or a # goes in
# double quotes. Environment variables of the same name win over this file.
# Nothing here is ever printed by the kit's scripts except the tracker name,
# url, project and email; tokens and passwords stay in this file.

# Which tracker the workflow talks to. "none" is valid: every ticket step is
# then skipped with a note and nothing else changes.
BEARING_TRACKER=none            # none | jira | gitlab | github | rest

# Which install profile this machine has; install.sh writes it and
# doctor reads it: minimal needs no third-party packs, standard and
# full need Superpowers, gstack and GSD Core.
BEARING_PROFILE=standard        # minimal | standard | full

# Which git host the repositories live on. brg-scaffold and brg-adopt copy
# only that host's CI and change template: gitlab (.gitlab-ci.yml, .gitlab/),
# github (.github/), or both. brg-adopt infers it from the origin remote when
# this is empty.
BEARING_GIT_HOST=both           # gitlab | github | both

# The status "brg-tracker close" moves a ticket to. Jira transitions to it,
# a REST tracker picks the status of that name, GitLab and GitHub apply it as
# a status label and close the issue.
BEARING_TRACKER_DONE_STATUS=Done

# Base url of the tracker. Examples per tracker:
#   rest            https://tracker.example.com (required; docs/TRACKERS.md)
#   jira            https://you.atlassian.net
#   gitlab          https://gitlab.example.com (default https://gitlab.com)
#   github          https://github.com (default; GitHub Enterprise: your host)
BEARING_TRACKER_URL=

# Where tickets live. REST tracker project key, Jira project key, GitLab
# project path (group/repo), GitHub owner/repo.
BEARING_TRACKER_PROJECT=

# The most pages "brg-tracker list" follows before it stops and says so.
BEARING_TRACKER_MAX_PAGES=20

# REST tracker or Jira login email. GitLab and GitHub ignore it.
BEARING_TRACKER_EMAIL=

# Jira API token, GitLab personal access token (scope api), GitHub token
# (scope repo). GitLab and GitHub may leave it empty and rely on `glab auth`
# or `gh auth` instead. A REST tracker takes its bearer token here.
BEARING_TRACKER_TOKEN=

# REST tracker password, traded for a token at its login endpoint (or set
# BEARING_TRACKER_TOKEN instead).
BEARING_TRACKER_PASSWORD=

# Optional: force the id prefix used in branch names and commit subjects,
# e.g. PROJ, GH, GL. When empty the adapter's own shape is used (Jira
# <project>-N, GitLab GL-N, GitHub GH-N, a REST tracker's own keys).
BEARING_TASK_ID_PREFIX=

# Optional: Jira issue type names when a site renamed the defaults.
# BEARING_JIRA_TYPES="epic=Epic,story=Story,task=Task,bug=Bug,testcase=Test"

# Git url of the Bearing fork developers install from. brg-scaffold and
# brg-adopt write it into each repository's CLAUDE.md and settings.
BEARING_KIT_REMOTE=

# Reverse-domain id for mobile bundle ids (android applicationId, iOS
# bundle identifier). brg-scaffold and brg-adopt use it as the --org default.
BEARING_ORG_ID=com.example

# AGENTS.md

The standard every AI coding agent follows in this repository (Claude Code,
Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot). It loads into every session, so it holds
only what applies on every turn; the skills carry each step's detail.

Use the strongest skill for a step, from any pack. A Bearing skill is the
choice only where nothing installed does the step better. Unsure which one:
`workflow` names the next step and its skill.

## Ground rules

Breaking one gets the change rejected, whatever else it does.

1. Never commit to `main` (or the trunk the snapshot names). Work on a task branch.
2. Never push, open a merge or pull request, merge, tag or deploy. Prepare the
   command and hand it to the engineer.
3. Never commit a secret, key, certificate or `.env` file, and never read one
   into context.
4. Never touch a production system, database or bucket, not even to read.
5. Never rewrite history: no amend, rebase, force-push, `reset --hard`.
6. Never weaken a guardrail to go green: no lint suppression, no `any` or
   `@ts-ignore`, no skipped test, no lowered threshold, no relaxed CI rule.
7. Never add a dependency nobody asked for; propose it with the reason.
8. Never invent an API, field, table, variable or command; find it in the code first.
9. Stay in scope. What you notice in passing goes under "Noticed", unfixed.
10. Report honestly: a check you did not run is "not run", never "passing".
11. No AI attribution in commits, requests or documents.
12. No em dashes in prose; rewrite the sentence.

## Working here

- Every change has a task id and a branch: `start-task` creates
  `feature|bugfix|chore|docs/<ID>-<PascalName>`. One task per session.
- Every command is a Makefile target; `make help` lists them and `make check`
  is the gate CI runs.
- Search before reading, open only what you located, and copy the shape,
  naming and tests of the closest existing example.
- More than three files, or a change to a schema, API contract, auth or
  billing: agree a plan before the first edit.
- A technology choice is never silent: `tech-decision` gives options and a
  recommendation, the engineer decides, `adr` records it.
- Commits are Conventional with the task id at the end of the subject:
  `feat(auth): add OTP lockout [TASK-142]`.
- State that must outlive the session: `.bearing/state/` via `session-handoff` (local, ignored); shared progress: `docs/progress/<ID>.md` (committed).
  Scratch: `.scratch/`. Nothing at the root such as `NOTES.md`.
- Done means `definition-of-done` passed with evidence. Code, database, testing and
  security rules live in `.claude/rules/` and load with the files they cover.

## Reporting

End every task in this shape: `## Changed` (path: what and why), `## Verified`
(the command and the tail of its output), `## Not done` (asked, not delivered,
why), `## Noticed` (seen in passing, not fixed). No full diffs, no restating
the task.

# CLAUDE.md

Claude Code specifics for this repository; the standard is AGENTS.md above.
Loaded into every session: keep this file under 40 lines.

```
Repository:   __REPO_NAME__ (__REPO_TYPE__)
Stack:        __STACK__
Databases:    __DATABASES__
Entrypoint:   __ENTRYPOINT__
Run, test:    make dev, make test; gate: make check
Git host:     gitlab | github | both (BEARING_GIT_HOST)
Tracker:      __TRACKER__ (BEARING_TRACKER; none is valid)
Trunk:        main (name develop here if this repository keeps one)
```

The Bearing plugin's hooks format and lint each edited file (`make
check-file` when the Makefile has it), add the task id from the branch,
refuse push, amend, rebase, merge, release and deploy commands, send you
back once when files you changed have not passed `make check`, and restore
the branch state and the user's last requests after compaction.
Permissions are in `.claude/settings.json`; `.claude/settings.local.json` may
add to them but must not loosen the deny list.

Plan mode for anything over three files or touching a schema, contract or
auth. On a third failed approach, stop and say so. Bound shell output with
`| tail -40`.

## Things the agent gets wrong in this repository

Add a line each time a mistake repeats; delete lines that stop applying.

# Code rules that hold in every stack (loaded when a source file is touched)

- Validate at the boundary, trust inside. Every request, response, message
  and config value is validated once, where it enters, with a schema the
  code derives its types from (Zod, Pydantic, Go structs with validation,
  Kotlin data classes with `require`, Swift `Codable` with checks).
- Errors carry context and are handled once. Wrap with what you were doing;
  map to a status code or user message at the edge; never swallow, never
  log and rethrow.
- No derived state stored. Compute it during render or on read. The server
  cache (TanStack Query, Room, Core Data) is the only copy of server data.
- No premature memoisation, caching or abstraction. Measure first.
- Names say what a thing is for. A function under thirty lines does one
  thing; a file under four hundred lines has one reason to change.
- Comments explain why, never what. Public functions get a one-line doc
  comment. TODOs carry the task id.
- Logs are structured, carry the request or trace id, and never contain a
  secret or PII.
- Feature flags default off; every flag has an owner and a removal task.
- Generated UI components under `src/components/ui/` (shadcn and similar)
  are regenerated from their source, never edited by hand; wrap or extend
  them in a sibling component instead.

---
paths:
  - "**/migrations/**"
  - "**/migration/**"
  - "**/*.sql"
  - "**/repository/**"
  - "**/repositories/**"
  - "**/db/**"
  - "**/alembic/**"
  - "**/prisma/**"

# Database rules (loaded when migrations, SQL or repositories are touched)

- Every schema change is a migration with a Down that is run in a test
  (`db-migration` scaffolds it). Long-running migrations run in batches
  and never hold an exclusive lock on a hot table.
- Postgres: no `SELECT *` in repository code; list the columns. Every new
  `WHERE` or `ORDER BY` shape records an index decision in the migration
  file's header comment. Add columns as nullable or with a default; backfill
  in batches; add `NOT NULL` in a later migration. `CREATE INDEX
  CONCURRENTLY` outside a transaction on any table over a million rows. No
  column type change in place on a hot table.
- ClickHouse: design `ORDER BY` for the read queries, not the inserts;
  partition by time; no `FINAL` on hot paths; deduplication is explicit
  (ReplacingMergeTree with a version column, or a dedup step) and
  documented in the migration.
- MongoDB: a JSON schema validator on every collection; an index for every
  query shape; arrays inside documents have a documented bound.
- Repositories own SQL and driver calls. Services receive domain types and
  never see a row, a cursor, a connection or a driver.
- Transactions are opened and closed in the service layer around the whole
  unit of work, passed to repositories, never opened inside a repository.
- Parameterised queries only. A string-built query is a finding.
- Timestamps are `timestamptz` (Postgres) or UTC epoch; ids are `uuid` or
  `bigint identity`, never application-generated integers.

- Test first when the behaviour is known (Superpowers
  `test-driven-development`). The test must be seen failing before the
  code that passes it exists.
- Every bug fix ships with the test that reproduces the bug against the
  unfixed code. Say so in a one-line comment with the task id.
- One behaviour per test, named after the behaviour: `rejects expired
  token`, not `testValidate2`.
- Arrange, act, assert, in that order, with a blank line between them. No
  logic in tests: no loops that decide what to assert, no conditionals.
- Unit tests for logic, integration tests against a real database in
  Docker for repositories (in a transaction rolled back after each test,
  never against shared state), an end-to-end test for every user-facing
  flow that matters (Playwright, Detox or Maestro, XCTest UI, Espresso).
- Deterministic: inject the clock, seed the random source, stub the
  network. A `sleep` in a test is a bug.
- Mirror the nearest existing test's fixtures and helpers. Do not invent a
  new fixture style for one file.
- Snapshot tests only for serialised output that is reviewed on change;
  never for component trees.
- Never `.only`, never `skip` without a task id and a reason.
- Run the narrowest selection that proves the change while working; the
  full `make check` once at the end.

  components without a permission, certificate pinning on money paths.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# pre-push: a person confirms on the terminal, branch name convention, no
# push to protected branches, and the full gate (make check) once before
# anything leaves the machine.
HOOK_NAME=pre-push
# shellcheck source=lib.sh
. "$(dirname "$0")/lib.sh"

remote="${1:-origin}"
branch="$(git branch --show-current)"

# Count the commits this push carries. git feeds one line per ref on stdin:
#   <local ref> <local sha> <remote ref> <remote sha>
# A remote sha of all zeros means the branch is new on the remote, so the
# count is every commit not already reachable from the remote's branches.
zero='0000000000000000000000000000000000000000'
refs=0; commits=0
while read -r local_ref local_sha remote_ref remote_sha; do
  [ -n "$local_ref" ] || continue
  refs=$((refs+1))
  if [ "$local_sha" = "$zero" ]; then
    continue # a delete carries no commits
  elif [ "$remote_sha" = "$zero" ]; then
    n="$(git rev-list --count "$local_sha" --not --remotes="$remote" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)"
  else
    n="$(git rev-list --count "$remote_sha..$local_sha" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)"
  fi
  commits=$((commits+n))
  hook_note "$local_ref -> ${remote_ref:-?}: $n commit(s)"
done
[ "$refs" -gt 0 ] || hook_fail "git handed the hook 0 refs; nothing to push"
[ "$commits" -gt 0 ] || hook_fail "0 commits to push; the remote already has everything on this ref"

# The engineer pushes; agents do not. A push must be confirmed by a person on
# the terminal within 60 seconds. A coding agent (any harness) runs without a
# controlling TTY, so the read fails and the push is refused. The bypass is
# for pipelines only and needs both a CI marker and an explicit opt-in.
in_ci=0
if [ "${CI:-}" = "true" ] || [ "${CI:-}" = "1" ] || [ -n "${GITLAB_CI:-}" ] || [ -n "${GITHUB_ACTIONS:-}" ]; then in_ci=1; fi
if [ "$in_ci" -eq 1 ] && [ "${BEARING_PUSH_CONFIRMED:-0}" = "1" ]; then
  hook_note "push confirmed by CI (BEARING_PUSH_CONFIRMED=1)"
elif { exec 3<>/dev/tty; } 2>/dev/null; then
  # fd 3 is the controlling terminal; opening it fails where there is none.
  printf 'Push %s to %s (%s commits)? Type the branch name to confirm (60 s): ' "$branch" "$remote" "$commits" >&3
  read -r -t 60 typed <&3 || typed=""
  exec 3>&-
  [ "$typed" = "$branch" ] || hook_fail "push not confirmed"
else
  hook_fail "no terminal to confirm the push; a person runs git push (CI sets CI=true and BEARING_PUSH_CONFIRMED=1)"
fi

case "$branch" in
  main|develop) hook_fail "direct push to $branch is not allowed; open a Merge Request" ;;
esac
printf '%s' "$branch" | grep -Eq "$BRANCH_RE" \
  || hook_fail "branch '$branch' does not match feature|bugfix|hotfix|chore|docs/<TASK-ID>-<PascalName> or release/vX.Y.Z"

# The gate. A repository on this standard has a Makefile with a check target;
# a missing one is a failure, not a note.
makefile=""
for m in Makefile makefile GNUmakefile; do [ -f "$m" ] && { makefile="$m"; break; }; done
[ -n "$makefile" ] || hook_fail "no Makefile; add a check target or run onboard-repo"
grep -qE '^check:' "$makefile" || hook_fail "no check target in $makefile; add a check target or run onboard-repo"
hook_note "running make check"
make check || hook_fail "make check failed; nothing was pushed"
hook_note "$commits commit(s) on $branch checked, gate passed"
exit 0

# commit-msg: Conventional Commit subject, task id present on task branches,
# no AI attribution trailer, no em dash, body wrapped.
HOOK_NAME=commit-msg
# shellcheck source=lib.sh
. "$(dirname "$0")/lib.sh"

msg_file="$1"
subject="$(sed -n '1p' "$msg_file")"
[ -n "$subject" ] || hook_fail "empty commit message"

case "$subject" in
  Merge\ *|Revert\ *|fixup!\ *|squash!\ *) hook_note "1 message checked (git-generated subject, rules not applied)"; exit 0 ;;
esac

printf '%s' "$subject" | grep -Eq "$COMMIT_RE" \
  || hook_fail "subject must be Conventional: 'type(scope): imperative summary [TASK-1]'. Got: $subject"

branch="$(git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null)"
task="$(printf '%s' "$branch" | grep -oE "$TASK_ID_RE" | head -1)"
if [ -n "$task" ] && ! printf '%s' "$subject" | grep -q "\[$task\]"; then
  hook_fail "branch carries $task; the subject must end with [$task]"
fi

grep -Eq "$AI_TRAILER_RE" "$msg_file" && hook_fail "AI attribution trailer found; a commit names a person who answers for it"
grep -q '—' "$msg_file" && hook_fail "em dash in commit message; rewrite the sentence"

long="$(sed -n '3,$p' "$msg_file" | grep -v '^#' | awk 'length > 100' | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
[ "$long" -eq 0 ] || hook_fail "$long body line(s) over 100 characters; wrap the body"
hook_note "1 message checked"
exit 0

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# pre-commit: format and lint the staged files only, block secrets and
# forbidden files. Fast: it never runs the whole suite.
HOOK_NAME=pre-commit
# shellcheck source=lib.sh
. "$(dirname "$0")/lib.sh"

# Staged paths into a bash array (bash 3.2: no mapfile). Paths may contain
# spaces, so every later command gets them through run_on, never unquoted.
files=()
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do files+=("$f"); done < <(staged_files0)
count=${#files[@]}
# Zero added, copied, modified or renamed files. A gate that examined nothing
# did not pass, so this fails unless the empty input is explained by one of
# three cases git itself treats as a real commit:
#   - deletions only: nothing to scan, and the deletions are counted;
#   - a merge whose result equals HEAD (MERGE_HEAD present; a clean merge
#     runs pre-merge-commit, not this hook);
#   - an empty commit the engineer asked for with --allow-empty, or a
#     reword with --amend, read from the git command line that ran the hook.
# Anything else (the hook run by hand, or `git commit` with nothing staged)
# fails with the count.
if [ "$count" -eq 0 ]; then
  deleted="$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=D | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
  [ "$deleted" -eq 0 ] || { hook_note "0 files to scan, $deleted deletion(s) staged; nothing else to check"; exit 0; }
  git_dir="$(git rev-parse --git-dir 2>/dev/null || echo .git)"
  [ ! -f "$git_dir/MERGE_HEAD" ] || { hook_note "0 staged files: merge commit whose tree equals HEAD"; exit 0; }
  # Only the git process that ran the hook counts; a shell whose command line
  # happens to mention the flag does not.
  # ps is missing in slim images and busybox's ps has no -o args= -p, so
  # read /proc first where it exists (Linux) and fall back to ps (macOS).
  parent=""
  if [ -r "/proc/$PPID/cmdline" ]; then
    parent="$(tr '\000' ' ' < "/proc/$PPID/cmdline" 2>/dev/null | sed 's/ *$//')"
  fi
  [ -n "$parent" ] || parent="$(ps -o args= -p "$PPID" 2>/dev/null || true)"
  case "${parent%% *}" in
    git|*/git|git.exe|*/git.exe)
      case " $parent " in
        *" --allow-empty "*) hook_note "0 staged files: empty commit requested with --allow-empty"; exit 0;;
        *" --amend "*) hook_note "0 staged files: --amend with no content change (reword)"; exit 0;;
      esac;;
  esac
  hook_fail "0 staged files, nothing checked (stage a change; use --allow-empty for an intentional empty commit)"
fi

# by_ext <regex>: the staged paths whose name matches, one per line.
by_ext() { printf '%s\n' "${files[@]}" | grep -E "$1" || true; }
# run_on <lines> <cmd...>: run cmd with the newline-separated paths as arguments.
run_on() { local list="$1"; shift; printf '%s\n' "$list" | tr '\n' '\0' | xargs -0 "$@"; }

# 1. Forbidden files.
bad="$(printf '%s\n' "${files[@]}" | grep -Ev '(^|/)\.env\.(example|sample|template)$' | grep -E '(^|/)\.env(\..*)?$|\.(pem|key|p12|jks|keystore|mobileprovision)$|service-account.*\.json$|google-services\.json$|GoogleService-Info\.plist$' || true)"
[ -z "$bad" ] || hook_fail "secret or credential file staged: $(printf '%s' "$bad" | tr '\n' ' ')"
root_notes="$(printf '%s\n' "${files[@]}" | grep -E '^(NOTES|SUMMARY|TODO)\.md$' || true)"
[ -z "$root_notes" ] || hook_fail "root notes file staged ($root_notes); use .scratch/ or docs/"
# The Claude Code sandbox holds 0-byte placeholders for protected paths in
# whichever directory a command runs (the root, or a package such as web/); a
# `git add -A` in that window stages them. A real .vscode or .idea is a
# directory and a real .mcp.json has content, so an empty regular file under
# one of these names, or under a .claude directory, is a placeholder.
placeholders=""
for f in "${files[@]}"; do
  named=0
  case "${f##*/}" in
    .vscode|.idea|.mcp.json|.gitmodules|.githooks|.ripgreprc|.bashrc|.bash_profile|.zshrc|.zprofile|.profile|.gitconfig) named=1;;
  esac
  case "/$f" in
    */.claude/agents|*/.claude/commands|*/.claude/hooks|*/.claude/launch.json|*/.claude/loop.md|*/.claude/output-styles|*/.claude/routines|*/.claude/scheduled_tasks.json|*/.claude/skills|*/.claude/workflows) named=1;;
  esac
  if [ "$named" = 1 ] && [ -f "$f" ] && [ ! -s "$f" ]; then placeholders="$placeholders $f"; fi
done
[ -z "$placeholders" ] || hook_fail "sandbox placeholder file(s) staged:$placeholders (empty, left by the Claude Code sandbox); unstage them: git restore --staged$placeholders"

# 2. Secret patterns in the added lines of the staged diff. Documented
# placeholders (.env.example and friends) and the hooks themselves, which
# spell the patterns out, are excluded from the scan.
secret_re='AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}'
secret_re="$secret_re|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----"
secret_re="$secret_re|ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}|github_pat_[A-Za-z0-9_]{20,}"
secret_re="$secret_re|glpat-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20}"
secret_re="$secret_re|sk-ant-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}|sk_live_[A-Za-z0-9]{16,}|sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{32,}"
secret_re="$secret_re|xox[baprs]-[A-Za-z0-9-]{10,}|xapp-[A-Za-z0-9-]{10,}"
secret_re="$secret_re|AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}"
secret_re="$secret_re|eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}"
scan_files="$(printf '%s\n' "${files[@]}" | grep -Ev '(^|/)\.env\.(example|sample|template)$|(^|/)\.githooks/' || true)"
if [ -n "$scan_files" ]; then
  hit="$(run_on "$scan_files" git diff --cached -U0 -- | grep -E '^\+' | grep -Ev '^\+\+\+' | grep -E "$secret_re" | head -1 || true)"
  [ -z "$hit" ] || hook_fail "a credential-shaped string is in the staged diff: $(printf '%s' "$hit" | cut -c1-40)..."
fi

# 3. Format and lint what is staged, by extension, with what the repo has.
go_files="$(by_ext '\.go$')"
if [ -n "$go_files" ] && command -v gofmt >/dev/null; then
  unformatted="$(run_on "$go_files" gofmt -l)"
  [ -z "$unformatted" ] || hook_fail "gofmt: $(printf '%s' "$unformatted" | tr '\n' ' ') (run make fix)"
fi
ts_files="$(by_ext '\.(ts|tsx|js|jsx|json|css|md)$')"
if [ -n "$ts_files" ] && [ -x node_modules/.bin/prettier ]; then
  run_on "$ts_files" node_modules/.bin/prettier --check --log-level warn || hook_fail "prettier: run make fix"
fi
py_files="$(by_ext '\.py$')"
if [ -n "$py_files" ]; then
  if command -v ruff >/dev/null; then
    run_on "$py_files" ruff format --check --quiet || hook_fail "ruff format: run make fix"
    run_on "$py_files" ruff check --quiet || hook_fail "ruff check failed"
  elif command -v uv >/dev/null && [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then
    run_on "$py_files" uv run --quiet ruff format --check --quiet || hook_fail "ruff format: run make fix"
  fi
fi
kt_files="$(by_ext '\.kts?$')"
if [ -n "$kt_files" ] && command -v ktlint >/dev/null; then
  run_on "$kt_files" ktlint || hook_fail "ktlint: run make fix"
fi
swift_files="$(by_ext '\.swift$')"
if [ -n "$swift_files" ] && command -v swiftformat >/dev/null; then
  run_on "$swift_files" swiftformat --lint || hook_fail "swiftformat: run make fix"
fi
tf_files="$(by_ext '\.tf$')"
if [ -n "$tf_files" ] && command -v terraform >/dev/null; then
  run_on "$tf_files" terraform fmt -check >/dev/null || hook_fail "terraform fmt: run make fix"
fi

# 4. Em dashes in prose files.
prose="$(by_ext '\.(md|txt)$')"
if [ -n "$prose" ]; then
  dashes="$(run_on "$prose" grep -l '—' 2>/dev/null || true)"
  [ -z "$dashes" ] || hook_fail "em dash in: $(printf '%s' "$dashes" | tr '\n' ' ')"
fi

hook_note "$count staged file(s) checked"
exit 0

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Shared helpers for the committed git hooks. Sourced by each hook.
set -u

hook_fail() { printf 'hook %s: %s\n' "${HOOK_NAME:-?}" "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
hook_note() { printf 'hook %s: %s\n' "${HOOK_NAME:-?}" "$*"; }

# Task id: an upper-case prefix, then one or more dash-number groups, in
# whatever shape the configured tracker uses: PREFIX-123, PREFIX-00-017.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Point git at the committed hooks. Idempotent. Run once per clone, or let
# `make setup` do it.
set -eu
root="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
# Write only when the value differs: Claude Code's sandbox mounts .git/config
# read-only, and an unconditional write failed make setup there.
if [ "$(git -C "$root" config --get core.hooksPath || true)" != ".githooks" ]; then
  git -C "$root" config core.hooksPath .githooks 2>/dev/null || {
    echo "could not set core.hooksPath=.githooks (.git/config is not writable); run: git config core.hooksPath .githooks" >&2; exit 1; }
fi
chmod +x "$root"/.githooks/commit-msg "$root"/.githooks/pre-commit "$root"/.githooks/pre-push
n=0
for h in commit-msg pre-commit pre-push; do [ -f "$root/.githooks/$h" ] && n=$((n+1)); done
[ "$n" -eq 3 ] || { echo "expected 3 hooks, found $n" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "git hooks installed: core.hooksPath=.githooks ($n hooks)"

# Contributing

How work moves through this repository. The standards themselves are in
`AGENTS.md`; this page is the procedure.

## First day

1. Clone, then `make setup`. It installs dependencies and points git at the
   committed hooks (`.githooks/`).
2. Install the workflow once per machine: follow `docs/INSTALL.md` in the
   Bearing repository (Claude Code plugin, or `harness-setup` for Cursor,
   Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot and others). Run `doctor` in this repo
   to confirm.
3. `make help` lists every target. `make dev` runs the app. `make check` is
   the gate CI runs; it prints `check: R gates run, S skipped` and fails
   when anything was skipped.

## A task, start to finish

1. Pick the task. Note its id: a ticket key from the tracker in the
   `CLAUDE.md` snapshot, or a chosen id such as `TASK-142` when there is
   no tracker.
2. `start-task TASK-142 <PascalName>` creates `feature/TASK-142-<PascalName>`
   from the trunk.
3. Vague task or boundary change: write the spec and plan first
   (Superpowers `brainstorming`, `writing-plans`, then `/plan-eng-review`).
4. Build test-first. Commit small, Conventional, with `[TASK-142]` at the
   end of the subject. The commit-msg hook enforces the shape.
5. `definition-of-done` when you think you are done. It walks the definition of done
   and asks for evidence.
6. `branch-review` for a stack-aware review; the harness's security review
   if you touched auth, payments, PII or external input.
7. `merge-request` runs `make check`, audits the commits and fills the merge
   request or pull request template into `.scratch/`. You push and open
   the request yourself; the pre-push hook asks you to type the branch
   name.
8. One peer and one lead approve. Address every thread; resolve none of
   your own.
9. Squash-merge with the Conventional subject. Delete the branch.
   `tracker-sync` moves the ticket, or skips with a note when there is none.

## Branches

Trunk-based by default: `main` is the trunk and what is in production.

- `feature|bugfix|chore|docs/<TASK-ID>-<PascalName>` from `main`, merged
  back to `main`.
- `hotfix/<TASK-ID>-<PascalName>` from `main`.
- `release/vX.Y.Z` only when a release needs stabilising; `release`
  prepares the changelog and the tag command, a person tags.

Teams that keep a `develop` integration branch say so in the `CLAUDE.md`
snapshot (`Trunk:` line); task branches then start from `develop`, only
`release/*` and `hotfix/*` merge to `main`, and hotfixes merge to both.

## Reviews

A review is findings, ranked, with file and line, each with the concrete
way it fails. Style is the formatter's job, not the reviewer's. Approve
only what you would answer for in an incident.

## Documentation

- A decision future readers will ask "why" about: `adr`.
- A new alert: `runbook` before the alert is enabled.
- An incident: `postmortem` within five working days.
- A new product event: `analytics-events` before the code emits it.

## Sessions with the agent

One task per session. `session-handoff` before you stop mid-task; the next
session starts with that state. Never let the agent push, merge or deploy;
the hooks stop it, and so should you.

# Security

## Reporting

Report a vulnerability to the lead in private (direct message or the
security channel), never in a public issue. Include the reproduction, the
impact and the commit. You will get an acknowledgement within one working
day.

## What every change must satisfy

1. Authorisation is per resource: every handler checks that the caller may
   act on this record.
2. Every input is validated at the boundary with a schema.
3. No secret in the repository, in logs, in error messages or in analytics.
   Configuration comes from the environment; `.env.example` lists every
   variable with a placeholder.
4. No credential-shaped file is ever committed; the pre-commit hook blocks
   the common ones, and the agent's settings deny reading them.
5. Dependencies are pinned. CI scans them; a known-vulnerable version blocks
   the pipeline.
6. Auth, payments, PII and external-input paths get gstack `/cso --diff`
   (or claude-security) before the MR, and before release a scan of the
   release commit that `vapt-report` writes up as the VAPT report. Critical and
   High findings are fixed before production.
7. Mobile: tokens live in the keychain or keystore; deep links are validated;
   no exported component without a permission; certificate pinning on money
   paths.
8. Infrastructure: least-privilege IAM, no public buckets, TLS everywhere,
   `terraform plan` reviewed before a person applies it.

## Incident

Declare early. Follow the runbook. Write the postmortem (`postmortem`)
within five working days. Blameless, with owned follow-ups.

# High Level Design: <system or feature>

<!-- Template guidance: every section below carries a comment saying what goes
     there (What), what a strong entry has (Good) and a one-line example
     (Example). Delete each comment when you fill its section. An HLD says
     what a system delivers, what it deliberately does not and where it
     breaks, for reviewers and for whoever writes the LLDs; it stops at the
     component boundary (no module layout, queries or class names). Every
     claim about the existing system comes from the code; anything else is
     prefixed "assumption:". Agree section 1 before writing section 2; the
     summary and the component table sit at the top but are written last.
     Every major section ends with a "**Risks this leaves open**" line and
     at least one bullet: a section with no risks has not been examined. -->

- Task: TASK-ID
- Author, date
- Status: Draft | Reviewed | Approved
- PRD: link
- ADRs: docs/architecture/decisions.md
- Tenets: docs/architecture/tenets.md

## Summary

<!-- What: two sentences a client can read alone: the shape of the system
     and the one or two choices that define it; then the system diagram
     path.
     Good: names the actual runtime, store and boundary, and what was
     deliberately left out; the diagram line is
     "Diagram: docs/architecture/diagrams/<Project>_SystemArchitecture_v<N>.svg",
     drawn by architecture-diagram from docs/architecture/architecture.json,
     with <N> the HLD version.
     Example: "One Go service on managed containers, backed by one Postgres,
     serves the web and mobile clients over one REST API; no broker and no
     second store. Invoices are reported by SQL over the domain tables, with
     no ETL in the first release." -->

## What gets built

<!-- What: one row per deployable component, in the columns
     Component | Kind | Stack | Responsibility | Repository.
     Good: Kind is frontend, backend, worker, infrastructure or data; Stack
     names the actual framework and libraries; Repository is the repo-plan
     name that builds it, "existing: <repo>" or "none (<reason>)".
     Example: "| Orders Api | backend | Go, net/http, pgx, goose | orders,
     invoices and the outbox worker; owns the one database | ShopOrdersApi |" -->

| Component | Kind | Stack | Responsibility | Repository |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

## 1. Goal and non-goals

<!-- What: what this delivers in three sentences, then a list of what it
     deliberately does not do. List the ids it serves (REQ-nnn, US-nn-nnn,
     ADR-nnnn); a pasted brief with no ids reads "Serves: unnumbered".
     Good: the user agreed this section before anything else was written;
     each non-goal is something a reader might reasonably expect.
     Example: "Non-goal: refunds; partial refunds stay manual in the admin
     console until US-07-002." -->

## 2. Users and flows

<!-- What: the actors and the two or three flows that matter, as numbered
     steps per actor.
     Good: two or three flows, not every screen; each step names the
     component it touches, and the story id it serves where there is one.
     Example: "3. Store admin uploads the price list CSV; the importer
     rejects the whole file on the first row with a bad SKU (US-02-004)." -->

## 3. Architecture

<!-- What: one mermaid diagram, then one paragraph per component:
     responsibility, owner, what it talks to and how; then the risks.
     Good: every component named was found in the code or is prefixed
     "assumption:"; a store, queue or auth choice points at its ADR or reads
     "ADR needed: <title>", never decided here; each risk names a failure
     the boundaries allow, not a generic worry.
     Example: "billing-worker (payments team): consumes invoice.issued from
     the jobs queue, calls the payment provider over HTTPS, writes payments.
     Risk: one process hosts the admin and the customer routes, so a panic in
     reporting takes down checkout." -->

**Risks this leaves open**

- <what can go wrong that this design does not fully solve>

## 4. Data

<!-- What: the entities, who owns each, the store, retention and the
     migrations the design implies; then the risks.
     Good: the store comes from an ADR or reads "ADR needed"; PII entities
     say so; the full model is left to data-model and linked.
     Example: "order: owned by checkout, Postgres (ADR-0004), kept 7 years;
     one new table, see docs/design/data-model.md." -->

**Risks this leaves open**

- <what can go wrong that this design does not fully solve>

## 5. Interfaces

<!-- What: every API, event and message this introduces or changes, with
     the location of its contract.
     Good: each entry names the contract path (an api/openapi.yaml path, a
     schema file, an event sheet) and says new or changed; the shapes live
     in the contract, not repeated here.
     Example: "POST /v1/orders (new), api/openapi.yaml; event order.placed
     v1 (new), docs/events/order.md." -->

## 6. External integrations

<!-- What: every third party on the runtime path, one paragraph or
     subsection each: what it is used for, what happens when it is down,
     slow or rate limited, and when its credential leaks; then what was
     deliberately not integrated; then the risks.
     Good: each failure says what the user sees and how it recovers; the
     credential names where it lives and who rotates it; a provider with no
     fallback says so plainly.
     Example: "Payment provider down: checkout returns the standard 503
     envelope and the cart is kept; webhooks are replayed from the
     provider's dashboard; key in the vault, rotated by the platform lead." -->

### Deliberately not integrated

<!-- What: the services a reader might expect and will not find, each with
     the reason.
     Good: every entry is something someone would plausibly add (an
     analytics SDK, a managed identity provider, a CRM); the reason names
     the ADR, the cost or the privacy rule that kept it out.
     Example: "- No crash-reporting SDK: it would capture screen state on the
     invoice view, which holds customer data (ADR-0003)." -->

- <service>: <why it was kept out>

**Risks this leaves open**

- <what can go wrong that this design does not fully solve>

## 7. Failure modes

<!-- What: one row per component: what fails, how it is noticed, what the
     user sees, how it recovers.
     Good: no blank cells; a cell nobody can fill is written UNDEFINED so
     the gap is visible and counted.
     Example: "| billing-worker | provider 5xx | payment_failures_total
     alert | 'Payment pending' banner | retry with backoff, 6 tries |" -->

## 8. Scaling and limits

<!-- What: expected load, the first bottleneck, and the number at which the
     design stops working; then the risks.
     Good: numbers with units and where they came from; "scales
     horizontally" is not a number and leaves the section unfinished.
     Example: "Peak 120 orders/min (last sale, Grafana); first limit is the
     stock row lock near 900/min; past that, shard by warehouse." -->

**Risks this leaves open**

- <what can go wrong that this design does not fully solve>

## 9. Security and privacy

<!-- What: the auth model, authorisation per resource, the PII touched and
     the secrets needed; then the risks.
     Good: authorisation says who may do what to which resource, not just
     "authenticated"; the auth model points at its ADR or "ADR needed".
     Example: "Orders: a customer reads only their own; store staff read
     their store's; secret PAYMENT_KEY_SECRET from the vault." -->

**Risks this leaves open**

- <what can go wrong that this design does not fully solve>

## 10. Observability

<!-- What: the logs, metrics, traces and alerts, each alert with its
     runbook name; then the risks.
     Good: named metrics and alerts with thresholds, not "we will add
     monitoring"; an alert without a runbook name is not finished.
     Example: "Alert OrderErrorRateHigh (5xx over 2% for 5 min), runbook
     docs/runbooks/order-errors.md." -->

**Risks this leaves open**

- <what can go wrong that this design does not fully solve>

## 11. Analytics

<!-- What: where product events come from, where they are stored, which
     business question each answers, and the reporting path; then the
     risks.
     Good: a table of question to source; product events kept apart from
     the audit trail; a count that is a lower bound says so; the store
     points at its ADR ("analytics store" key) or reads "ADR needed".
     Example: "| Do customers abandon checkout? | checkout_started events
     against orders rows; a lower bound, lost on network failure |" -->

**Risks this leaves open**

- <what can go wrong that this design does not fully solve>

## 12. Rollout and rollback

<!-- What: the flags, the phases, the migration order and how to back out
     at each phase; then the risks.
     Good: a way back is written for every phase, not only the last; the
     migration order is explicit when schema and code ship separately;
     work in flight at a cutover (jobs already queued in the old path,
     rows mid-state) has a stated fate in both directions.
     Example: "Phase 2: flag orders_v2 on for 3 pilot stores; back out by
     turning the flag off; new rows stay and v1 ignores them." -->

**Risks this leaves open**

- <what can go wrong that this design does not fully solve>

## 13. Outside the standard stack

<!-- What: every technology in this design that is not a default in the
     tech-decision catalogue, each with the ADR that chose it and the sign-off
     it needs from the Architect or the Engineering Manager.
     Good: one line per technology, deduplicated across ADRs, with the
     reviewer and the state of the sign-off; when there is none, write
     "None: every technology is a catalogue default".
     Example: "- Caddy (compute, ADR-0007): Architect sign-off pending." -->

## 14. Repository plan

<!-- What: the repositories that build the components above, mirrored from
     docs/architecture/repo-plan.json, as Repository | Path | Stack id |
     Responsibility | Apps.
     Good: names are <Project><Component> PascalCase; paths sit under the
     Client, Server or Infrastructure subgroup; the stack id is one the kit
     scaffolds, so new-repo can create each entry as written.
     Example: "| ShopOrdersApi | Shop/Server/ShopOrdersApi | go-api | the one
     backend service | none |" -->

## 15. Decisions and conflicts

<!-- What: the count of ADRs and of settled conflicts, pointing at
     docs/architecture/decisions.md, and every ADR still needed.
     Good: each contradiction found between the ADRs, the stories and the
     data model is settled in the register, not argued here; an open
     conflict blocks Approved.
     Example: "12 ADRs, 5 conflicts settled (2 Proposed), 0 open; ADR
     needed: search store." -->

## 16. What the review found

<!-- What: the independent review by critic, which wrote none of this:
     a "Reviewed by:" line, then one "### <SEVERITY>: <title>" per finding
     graded BLOCKER, MAJOR, MINOR or NIT, each with what is wrong,
     "Conflicts with:" (the ADRs, sections, stories or tables it
     contradicts), "Fix:" and "Status: open | fixed (<where>) | accepted
     (<who>)".
     Good: BLOCKER means it cannot be built as written, MAJOR costs weeks;
     the HLD is not Approved while a BLOCKER is open.
     Example: "### BLOCKER: ADR-0005 keeps secrets in a manager ADR-0007
     excludes / Conflicts with: ADR-0005, ADR-0007 / Fix: move the signing
     key to the per-environment config ADR-0009 set up / Status: open" -->

## 17. Open questions and assumptions

<!-- What: each open question and each "assumption:" from the sections
     above, with an owner and a date.
     Good: an owner who can answer it and the date it blocks; a question
     with no owner is counted as missing in the output contract.
     Example: "assumption: stores never share customers across tenants;
     owner Priya (product), answer by 2026-10-05." -->

# Low Level Design: <component>

<!-- Template guidance: every section below carries a comment saying what goes
     there (What), what a strong entry has (Good) and a one-line example
     (Example). Delete each comment when you fill its section. An LLD turns
     one component of an agreed HLD into files, types, queries and MRs, for
     the engineers who build it and the reviewers of those MRs. It never
     reopens the goal, the store or the boundaries; a change to any of them
     is an ADR and an HLD edit first. Put the HLD's ids and the AC-US-nn-nnn-k
     ids the tests cover at the top. -->

- Task: TASK-ID, HLD: link, ADRs: links
- Author, date, status

## 1. Scope

<!-- What: the one component this covers and its boundary, in two
     sentences.
     Good: exactly one component; a scope that spans two gets two LLDs. With
     no HLD, the boundary comes from the code and is confirmed with the user.
     Example: "The slot allocator in internal/booking/: it reserves and
     releases slots; payment and notifications stay outside it." -->

## 2. Module layout

<!-- What: the packages and files, and what each owns, mirroring the stack
     skill's layout rules.
     Good: existing files are real paths; new ones are marked (new); a file
     expected to pass 400 lines is split here, not later.
     Example: "internal/booking/allocator.go (new): Reserve and Release,
     owns the slot state machine; about 180 lines." -->

## 3. Types and schemas

<!-- What: the domain types, the boundary schemas (request, response,
     event, config) and the one place each is validated.
     Good: each schema names its single validation point; HTTP shapes point
     at api/openapi.yaml rather than being repeated here.
     Example: "ReserveRequest: POST /v1/slots/reserve in api/openapi.yaml,
     validated once in internal/http/booking_handler.go." -->

## 4. Sequence

<!-- What: one mermaid sequenceDiagram per flow, with an alt block for
     every error branch.
     Good: the error branches are drawn, not described in a sentence; a flow
     with no error branch carries the line "UNDEFINED error branch".
     Example: "alt slot already taken: Allocator->>Handler: ErrSlotTaken;
     Handler->>Client: 409 slot_taken." -->

## 5. Data access

<!-- What: each query with the index it uses and its query shape, the
     transactions and their boundaries, and the migrations in order as
     db-migration names.
     Good: every query names its index or is marked a known full scan with
     the row count ("add index later" is a query without one); each
     transaction says what is inside, what is not and why.
     Example: "Find free slots: WHERE clinic_id = $1 AND starts_at >= $2,
     idx_slots_clinic_starts; migration add_slots_hold_until (expand)." -->

## 6. Errors

<!-- What: each error type, where it is created, where it is wrapped and
     where it is mapped to a status code or user message.
     Good: file-level locations for all three; HTTP errors use the repo's
     JSON error envelope from openapi-spec.
     Example: "ErrSlotTaken: created in allocator.go, wrapped in
     service.go, mapped to 409 slot_taken in booking_handler.go." -->

## 7. Configuration

<!-- What: every variable, its default, and what happens when it is
     missing.
     Good: each variable appears in .env.example; any that does not is
     listed here as missing from it.
     Example: "| SLOT_HOLD_SECONDS | 300 | missing: the default applies and
     startup logs a warning |" -->

## 8. Tests

<!-- What: the unit, integration and end-to-end tests this design needs,
     by name.
     Good: each test has a real name and is tagged with the AC-US-nn-nnn-k
     or TC-nnnn it proves; a category like "unit tests for the allocator"
     is not a name.
     Example: "TestReserve_SecondCallerGetsSlotTaken (unit), proves
     AC-US-02-003-2." -->

## 9. Work breakdown

<!-- What: the tasks in order, each one MR, naming the files it touches,
     the tests it adds and an estimated line count.
     Good: no item over 400 lines; every MR leaves make check green, so an
     item that only compiles after the next one is two items in the wrong
     order. Zero items means the design is not done.
     Example: "2. Allocator and its unit tests: allocator.go (new),
     allocator_test.go (new); about 260 lines." -->

## 10. Assumptions

<!-- What: every statement above that is not proven from the code, the HLD
     or an ADR, one per line with the prefix "assumption:"; the critic's
     three weakest claims go here too when it ran.
     Good: each names what would confirm or break it and who can answer;
     the count here is the "Assumptions: K" line in the report.
     Example: "assumption: at most 40 reservations a second at the 07:00
     peak (from the HLD scaling section); confirm from the March access
     logs, owner: platform on-call." -->

# Runbook: <alert name exactly as it fires>

<!-- Template guidance: every section below carries a comment saying what goes
     there (What), what a strong entry has (Good) and a one-line example
     (Example). Delete each comment when you fill its section. A runbook is
     read at 3 a.m. by an on-call engineer who did not write the service:
     one alert, one runbook, file named as the alert fires
     (docs/runbooks/<alert-name>.md). Every command is copy-pasteable with
     placeholders in angle brackets; no credentials and no production
     database hostnames (point at the secret manager and the inventory). -->

- Service:
- Severity:
- Owner (team, on-call rotation):
- Dashboard:
- Last verified: not run (or YYYY-MM-DD with the diagnosis output quoted below)

## What this alert means

<!-- What: one paragraph: the condition, the threshold, the window, and why
     we alert on it.
     Good: quotes the rule's expression or names the rule file
     (monitoring/alerts/api.yaml), or says "alert rule: not in this
     repository"; says which user promise the threshold protects.
     Example: "Fires when 5xx responses exceed 1 percent of API requests for
     5 minutes (monitoring/alerts/api.yaml, ApiErrorRateHigh); at that rate
     the monthly error budget is gone in under two days." -->

## User impact

<!-- What: what a user experiences while this is firing.
     Good: names the journey and the symptom the user sees (an error page,
     a spinner, a missing email), and who is spared; not "service degraded".
     Example: "Customers see 'Payment could not be completed' at checkout;
     browsing and basket still work." -->

## Diagnosis

<!-- What: numbered steps, each the exact command or dashboard panel, and
     what a healthy versus an unhealthy result looks like.
     Good: every command runs as pasted once the angle-bracket placeholders
     are filled; each step says what to conclude from the output. When the
     steps were run for "Last verified", quote each step's output under it.
     Example: "1. kubectl -n <namespace> get pods -l app=api. Healthy: all
     Running, restarts 0. Unhealthy: CrashLoopBackOff, go to Remediation 2." -->

## Remediation

<!-- What: numbered steps for the common causes, most likely first.
     Good: ordered by likelihood; each step says how to confirm it worked
     (the panel or command and the value to expect); the person runs it,
     nothing is automatic.
     Example: "1. Last deploy is the cause: follow Rollback. Confirm: the 5xx
     panel on the API dashboard drops under 0.1 percent within 5 minutes." -->

## Rollback

<!-- What: how to back out the last change if that is the cause.
     Good: names the mechanism (a revert and redeploy, a flag turned off, a
     migration Down) with the exact command, and says when rollback is not
     safe (a migration that dropped a column).
     Example: "make deploy TAG=<previous release tag>; if the release ran a
     migration, run its Down first: make migrate-down STEPS=1." -->

## Escalation

<!-- What: who to page when the steps above do not resolve it, and after how
     long.
     Good: names a rotation or team, never a person, with the time limit and
     the channel.
     Example: "After 30 minutes without recovery, page the payments-oncall
     rotation in PagerDuty and post in #inc-payments." -->

## After

<!-- What: what to record, and whether a postmortem is required.
     Good: says where the timeline goes (the incident doc), that this
     runbook is updated with what the responders actually did (commands
     that worked, a signal that misled, a missing step), and when a
     postmortem is due.
     Example: "Record the timeline in docs/postmortems/<date>-<title>-incident.md;
     sev 1 to 3 need a postmortem (postmortem) within five working days." -->
